title_original: ‘The Cycle Of Love’ To Return To Cinemas For One-Day Only Engagement: Extraordinary Romantic Tale From Director Orlando Von Einsiedel
editorial_title_zh: 《爱之循环》将重返影院进行仅限一天的放映：来自导演奥兰多·冯·爱因舍德尔的非凡浪漫传奇

"“我们并非所有人都有命中注定的缘分，或是在孩童时得到过预言，但我们都有希望、梦想与抱负，”冯·恩西德尔指出，“但要实现这些，你必须付出努力。我认为这是这部电影核心所传达的一个极其鼓舞人心的信息。这是一个生活极为艰难的男人，他决定改变现状，并承担了巨大的风险。我们或许无法骑自行车6,000英里去改变生活，但我们都可以做些什么来达成自己的梦想。”", "translated": true}, article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Fresh from earning two nominations for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards , The Cycle of Love is cycling back into theaters.

The romantic documentary directed by Oscar winner Orlando von Einsiedel and executive produced by Priyanka Chopra Jonas will play for one-day only on November 1, which the distributor is calling a special “date night” screening event. It’s booked in locations nationwide from New York to Los Angeles, and even further west to Hawaii. The film, which recounts the extraordinary love story of PK — an “untouchable” young Indian artist — and Lotta, “a Swedish adventurer in search of magic, whose meeting was written in the stars from [PK’s] birth,” becomes available on TVOD starting November 2, on Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, and YouTube.

The Cyle of Love won the Artemis Rising Foundation Award for Social Impact at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York and audience awards at the Middleburg Film Festival in Virginia and the Indie Meme Film Festival in Austin, TX. At the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, it’s nominated for Best Director, recognizing von Einsiedel, and Best Cinematography, recognizing DoP Franklin Dow.

Watch on Deadline

“In 1977, PK, a 23-year-old Delhi street artist from a poor, ‘untouchable’ family, picked up a handful of paintbrushes and a second-hand bicycle and set off across 6000 miles and nearly a dozen countries,” notes a synopsis. “His mission: to find Lotta, the woman who had captured his heart on a visit to India.

“PK knew their meeting was fate. When he was still a baby, an astrologer left his parents with a prophecy: ‘You will marry a girl who is not from the village, not even from this country, she will be musical, own a jungle and be born under the sign of the ox.’ Lotta was born in May and she played the recorder and piano. When PK asked her if she owned a jungle, she replied, ‘not a jungle, but a forest.’ He knew this was his destiny. Charmed by his smile, creativity and gentleness, Lotta accepted his offer to show her around India and, over her two-month visit, they fell hopelessly in love, despite caste, nationality, and everything else.”

Von Einsiedel won his Academy Award for The White Helmets (2016) and earned an Academy Award nomination for Virunga (2014). His additional directing credits include The Lost Children (2024), co-directed by Jorge Duran and Lali Houghton; the documentary series Heart of Invictus (2023), and the short film Lost and Found (2019).

In a recent interview with Deadline, von Einsiedel told us about the origins of The Cycle of Love .

“I was in Sweden and I was giving a talk at an event and two young people, very smiley young people, came up to me and handed me a book and said, ‘This is a book about our parents’ story and we know your work a little bit. And if you like this story and are interested, would you consider making a film about it?’” the filmmaker recalled. “When somebody approaches you cold and says, ‘This is a great story,’ it sadly isn’t always a great story. So, I didn’t have the highest hopes in the world, but I read the book a number of weeks later and immediately knew I’d been an idiot for not being more enthusiastic. And the story blew my mind and it’s about magic and destiny and love and adventure and the kindness of strangers. And I immediately got back in touch and said, ‘Hello, do you remember me?’ And luckily, they did remember me.”

The film includes extensive dramatizations immersing viewers in this almost unimaginable story. Von Einsiedel cast actor Chirag Lobo as young PK, and actress Mina Dale as young Lotta.

“I learned very quickly there wasn’t much archive footage… PK unfortunately didn’t have a documentary crew following him in 1977,” von Einsiedel said. “Normally, that [cuts] a documentary off at its knees. And I found that very scary, but it was kind of freeing and wonderful in a way to try and problem-solve how to overcome this.”

The film becomes a road movie, with the director casting people he met in the course of filming — non-professional actors — to take part in it. Von Einsiedel says his approach was inspired by several acclaimed directors.

“I suppose I’ve borrowed enormously from amazing filmmakers like Abbas Kiarostami, Chloé Zhao, Jonas Poher Rasmussen and the Ross Brothers, all these brilliant people who blended documentary and scripted,” he said. “I’ve tried to stand on their shoulders and try something different.”

PK’s story of perseverance — receiving a sign about his future and then undertaking a journey to make that vision a reality — has touched audiences around the world.

“We don’t all have destiny written for us or given a prophecy as children, but we all have hopes and dreams and ambitions,” von Einsiedel observed. “But to make those happen, you have to work at them. And I think that’s a really inspiring message at the heart of this film. Here’s a man who had a very difficult life and he decided he was going to change it and took an enormous risk. And we might not be able to cycle 6,000 miles to change our lives, but we can all do something to achieve our dreams.”

He added, “There’s a line PK says as well: ‘We can choose which story to believe about ourselves.’ I think that’s such a powerful line because PK had been told all his life that he was polluted, he was dirty, he was nothing, and he chose not to believe any of that and achieved extraordinary things because of that.”

The Cycle of Love is a Grain Media and Kalabati Pictures production, in Association with BD4, Tudip Entertainment and AMPL, Artemis Rising Foundation, Grace Labs, Waldesfriede Films and Purple Pebble Pictures. The film is produced by Harri Grace, Chloe Leland, Emelie Mahanandia von Schedvin, and Karl Mahanandia von Schedvin.

Executive producers are Priyanka Chopra Jonas, Anne Carey, Adriana Banta, Jorge Villon, Abhijeet Chhabra, Dan Silver, Ryan Harrington, Geralyn Dreyfous, Emily Goldner, Chris Silvestri, Mark Roden, Melony and Adam Lewis, Michael Humphries, Regina K. Scully, Lekha Singh, Cristina Ljungberg, Victoria Steventon, The Reilly Family, Danielle Turkov, and Amy Shepherd.

title_original: Youthful Edward Hopper Oil Paintings Revealed to Be Copies of Other Artists’ Work
editorial_title_zh: 年轻时的爱德华·霍珀油画被证实为其他艺术家作品的临摹
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这一发现发表在路易斯·沙德威克为该艺术家撰写的新传记中。

article_text:
An excerpt from Louis Shadwick’s new Edward Hopper biography, published in the Art Newspaper Tuesday, reveals that all six of the artist’s early oil paintings are in fact copies of other artists’ works, rather than Hopper’s own original compositions. Hopper made the paintings in a studio in his family’s home in Nyack, New York, when he was a teenager, before attending art school in New York City.

The works were discovered in the attic of Hopper’s childhood home in the late 1960s, after the artist’s death, by the Reverend Arthayer R. Sanborn. Sanborn, a Baptist minister, lived down the street from Hopper’s family and had cared for Hopper’s sister and wife. He somewhat controversially acquired a trove of Hopper memorabilia—letters, photographs, notebooks, and the like—along with early paintings and drawings, from the Hopper house in Nyack as well as the couple’s Greenwich Village apartment. Much of this archive is now owned by the Whitney Museum of American Art.

According to Shadwick, Sanborn also gave some of these early oil paintings new, misleading titles, and assumed Hopper had conceived of the compositions himself, inspired by his surroundings in Nyack. One example was titled Old Ice Pond at Nyack by Sanborn, and for decades was thought to depict the skating pond near where Hopper grew up; Sanborn called another Rowboat on Hudson , similarly connecting it to Hopper’s environs. Both, it turns out, are copies Hopper made from instructional images reproduced in color plates in the publication Art Interchange . Old Ice Pond at Nyack was a copy of a painting by Bruce Crane called A Winter Sunset (December 1890 issue), and Rowboat on Hudson (or Rowboat in Rocky Cove , as it was also known) was a copy of a watercolor titled Lake View by an unidentified artist (February 1891).

Other examples of early oil paintings mentioned by Shadwick include Country Road (copied from A Landscape Study in Color by John Francis Murphy), Ships (copied from Marine View by Edward Moran), and Clipper Ship Being Towed by Tug (copied from Stormy Voyage by Fred Pansing). Hopper painted all of these in the late 1890s, when he was around 15 or 16 years old; most are signed with his name or initials.

Shadwick does not think Hopper was attempting to mislead anyone regarding the nature of these early paintings. Rather, “the signatures suggest the artist’s youthful pride in his earliest achievements in oil that were never intended to be seen publicly.” More than a “gotcha,” Shadwick’s discovery acts as a revision to the way Hopper’s early artistic output is perceived. His gift for painting did not, it turns out, emerge suddenly during adolescence with no instruction, nor was he first exposed to American art movements in art school.
excerpt_original: The discovery is published in a new biography on the artist by Louis Shadwick.

article_text:
Japanese animated phenomenon “ Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island ” held the No. 1 position at the South Korean box office over the weekend of Oct. 30–Nov. 1, securing its third consecutive weekend atop the rankings.

According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Toho-distributed fantasy release generated $1.7 million from 221,651 admissions across 1,167 screens, claiming 32.1% of the weekend market. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the popular manga by Nagano, the animated blockbuster has reached a cumulative gross of $20.1 million from 2,583,851 total admissions since its Sep. 30 rollout.

Related Stories

Why Did Netflix Boot Bela Bajaria?

How Netflix’s Messy Transition Will Rock Hollywood: Looking at You, NBCU

Sony Pictures and TriStar’s survival thriller “ Heart of the Beast ” opened in second place, pulling in $1.2 million from 162,790 admissions across 1,106 screens to capture 23% of theatrical revenue. Since opening mid-week on Oct. 28, the title has accumulated $1.5 million from 215,237 admissions.

By4M Studio and Barunson E&A’s workplace comedy “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng” debuted in third place, taking in $326,609 from 44,799 admissions across 677 screens for 6.09% of the market. The directorial debut of screenwriter Lee Yong-jae stars Lee Sun-bin, Yoo Jae-myung, Kim Young-min, and Jeon Seok-ho, following a high school language teacher unexpectedly sequestered into the top-secret 40-day test-writing committee for the national college entrance examination. Following its premiere at the Busan International Film Festival and an Oct. 28 commercial bow, the comedy has grossed $505,208 from 71,767 viewers.

Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “ The Assassin(s) ” placed fourth in its sixth frame, collecting $307,719 from 41,265 admissions across 620 screens for 5.7% of receipts. Distributed by Hive Media Corp and starring Yu Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho, the drama reconstructs the August 15, 1974 assassination attempt on President Park Chung-hee. Despite ongoing legal complaints and protests from conservative civic groups alleging historical distortion over its portrayal of state inquiry contradictions, the title lifted its cumulative total to $25.5 million from 3,448,036 admissions since its Sep. 23 launch.

Anime re-release “Attack on Titan: Crimson Arrows” placed fifth, grossing $266,616 from 30,263 admissions across 233 screens. The theatrical re-issue of the 2014 feature pushed its updated cumulative haul to $547,187 from 72,324 admissions.

CJ ENM’s gambling drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” took sixth place, earning $208,310 from 26,650 admissions across 498 screens. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the comic-adapted franchise officially crossed the two-million-ticket threshold, reaching $15.7 million from 2,055,522 total viewers.

CJ Entertainment’s psychological thriller “Paradise Lost,” directed by Yeon Sang-ho and starring Kim Hyun-joo and Bae Hyun-sung, placed seventh on the admissions chart with $124,104 from 17,053 admissions across 593 screens, bringing its cume to $1 million from 151,429 admissions.

Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” placed eighth in admissions with 16,641 viewers across 444 screens, though it generated a higher revenue gross of $140,321. The film has accumulated $899,915 from 115,464 admissions.

Universal’s tentpole “The Odyssey” took ninth place in its 13th weekend, adding $108,833 from 13,332 admissions across 254 screens. The film took 2.02% of the frame, lifting its cumulative total to $106.4 million from 12,335,377 admissions since its Aug. 5 opening.

Rounding out the top ten, Japanese romantic drama “You, Like a Star” debuted with $77,264 from 10,091 admissions across 154 screens. Directed by Michihito Fujii and starring Ryusei Yokohama and Suzu Hirose as young lovers bound by shared hardship on an island in the Seto Inland Sea, the film has grossed $146,509 from 20,478 admissions since its Oct. 28 release.

The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $5.3 million, down from last week’s $5.6 million.

article_text:
Still Life, Then and Now

★★★★☆

Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.

This brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.

When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.

The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.

Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.

Robilant , London, until 18 December

Paul Pfeiffer: Pasodoble

★★★★☆

Panting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.

This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.

It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.

Thomas Dane Gallery , London, until 19 December

Flip In: Ebecho Muslimova

★★★★☆

Ebecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.

In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.

Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.

All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.

Bernheim , London, until 28 November

Rosalind Nashashibi: Gaza Apollo

★★★☆☆

Back in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.

Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.

Art and design

article_text:
Film Review

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

“You Can See Everything” is toted as a documentary, but is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian?

You Can See Everything (2026), dir. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (image courtesy A24)

Editor’s Note: This review contains spoilers.

As an art historian, it's hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything . I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one?

Artist Martha Wilson recently defined performance art as an intervention that unfolds in real time, often placing the artist’s body at the center of the action. The genre has long tested the limits of what an artist’s body can do, and what an audience will tolerate: Chris Burden had himself shot with a .22-caliber gun in “Shoot” (1971); Yoko Ono invited audience members to cut away her clothing in “Cut Piece” (1964); and Carolee Schneemann pulled a scroll from her vagina in “Interior Scroll” (1975). These works differ considerably, but each makes the artist’s actions and the responses they provoke central to the work.

Fielder, too, puts himself in the middle of things. In You Can See Everything, he spends 34 days filming and questioning Holmes, her partner Billy Evans, and their two children. Eventually, he moves into the guesthouse of their California beachfront rental, just before Holmes begins her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors and patients of Theranos, whose blood-testing technology falsely claimed it could run a wide range of tests on a few drops of blood. The couple frames their participation as an act of “radical transparency,” hoping to persuade the public that Holmes is innocent. They chose Fielder as their documentarian, they explain, because he “thinks outside the box” just like they do. Game recognizes game.

Fielder’s move turns observation into participation. His proximity to the family becomes part of the experiment, shaping the behavior he records. In one scene, he films himself lurking at a distance as Billy and Holmes embrace. In another, he sits close to Holmes on a couch; a hand strokes her shoulder, and for a moment it seems to belong to Fielder, until the camera reveals Billy on the other side. But the film invites us to imagine a silent intimacy growing between Holmes and Fielder that it never confirms. Elsewhere, Holmes texts flirtatiously, “fyi you can totally see everything.” The title begins to feel less like a promise of transparency and more like provocation: Who is watching who? What does each person want seen?
excerpt_original: “You Can See Everything” is toted as a documentary, but is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian?

article_text:
The Atlas Workshops , Marrakech Film Festival’s project development platform, has named Brazilian director Kleber Mendonça Filho as the patron of its 9th edition and unveiled the 30 projects invited to participate.

The award-winning The Secret Agent filmmaker follows in the footsteps of Cristian Mungiu and Jeff Nichols , in a role which will see him mentor the filmmakers in attendance.

Mendonça Filho was at Marrakech last year while on the awards trail with The Secret Agent , which won best director in Cannes and then went on to clinch two Golden Globes and four Oscar nominations.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Marion Cotillard Unveiled As 2026 Marrakech Film Festival Jury President

'The Secret Agent' Director Kleber Mendonça Filho On His Film's Four Oscar Nominations: "It's So Good To See Casting Recognized"

“Last year, during my Conversation at the festival, I was asked whether I had ever planned to shoot a film in this city. Serving as the patron of the Atlas Workshops makes me feel as though I’m witnessing, right before my eyes, the birth of new films,” said the director, whose credits also include Aquarius (2016), and Bacurau on the Map (2019).

“I am delighted to receive this invitation. Listening to new ideas and understanding the aspirations of new generations of filmmakers is a source of inspiration for my own work.”

Selected from 410 submitted projects, the workshops will present 30 projects hailing from 14 countries, spanning Algeria, Cabo Verde, Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine, Rwanda, Senegal, Sudan, Syria, and Tunisia.

The lineup is split between 14 projects in development, 11 films in production or post-production, and five projects in the Atlas Close-Ups section, which is dedicated to Moroccan cinema. (scroll down for full list)

The projects in development include new projects from a host of directors who have already made their mark, including Amjad Abu Alala ( You Will Die at Twenty ), Laila Abbas ( Thank You for Banking with Us ), Meryem Benm’Barek ( Sofia; Behind the Palm Trees ), Sofia Alaoui ( Animalia ), and Yasmine Benkiran ( Queens ).

“We have a strong presence of strong female Moroccan directors,” said Atlas Workshops head Hédi Zardi, referring to Benm’Barek, Alaoui and Benkiran.

There are also first features by buzzy newcomers including Sarra Ryma, whose short film What Do The Maknines Dream Of played in Cannes Critics’ Week this year, while Zardi also noted the presence of French Senegalese filmmaker Dyana Gaye, with her first film in a decade, a Dakar-set musical entitled Studio Kébé.

“The aim is to have a good mix of discoveries and features by more established directors,” said Zardi.

Four of the 11 projects in the production or post-production selection previously participated in the Atlas Workshops at the development stage: Samuel Ishimwe’s Seasons of the Weary Kind (Rwanda), Alaa Eddine Aljem’s Eldorado (Morocco), Yoro Mbaye’s Fagadaga (Senegal), and Ismaël El Iraki’s Wolfmother (Morocco).

“It shows a continuity in our work,” commented Zardi, noting the presence of emerging talents such as Lebanese director Jessy Moussallem, who will attend with Faux Bijoux , an extension of her award-winning short of the same name.

“She has just started shooting and will show us the first images straight from the shoot at Atlas,” said Hardi.

Commenting on the Atlas Close-Ups lineup focused purely on Moroccan films, Hardi highlighted to the diversity of the selection, ranging from hybrid documentary Amar Made His Dream Come True , to audience-driven B512, The Man Who Forgot To Die and poetic drama The Cemetery’s Birds .

Atlas Station, supporting emerging Moroccan producers and directors, will support eight local producers and showcase five short film projects.

Founded in 2018, the Atlas Workshops is enjoying a vintage year on the festival front thanks to past participants such as Congo Boy and Strawberries, which premiered in Cannes Un Certain Regard; Furies, which played in Venice; Bardi , which debuted in New York; and Ego Reach We All , which screened in Locarno.

Atlas Workshops is one prong of Marrakech’s Atlas Programs banner, which gathers the professional initiatives of the Marrakech International Film Festival.

Alongside the Atlas Workshops and Atlas Station, Atlas Press supports the development of film criticism, while the Atlas Distribution Meetings bring together some 60 professionals from Africa, the Arab world, and Europe to foster networking and the circulation of films. The Atlas Distribution Awards round out this initiative by providing support for the distribution of films.

The Atlas Workshops, Atlas Station, and Atlas Distribution Meetings take place in Marrakech from November 22 to 26, while Atlas Press takes place from November 23 to 27, 2026.

Prior to the physical meeting in Marrakech, the Atlas Workshops will hold online sessions from November 2 to 6 to get the participants up to date with the latest industry developments and trends for independent film.

"从小就喜欢书的濑名在最后一个展区介绍了对她产生巨大影响的书籍。其中一本是她一生的恩师武井武雄的书，据说她特别喜欢《玩具箱》。另一本是海外的儿童绘本《长发彼得》（海因里希·霍夫曼），她对父亲赠予的这本书格外珍视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "高中时期她便立志成为一名画家，但由于母亲管教严厉，未能如愿考入美术大学，最终进入日本银行工作。午休时她四处拜访出版社推销插图，并开始在少女杂志等刊物上发表作品。19岁时，她拜童画家武井武雄为师。在潜心学习的同时，她还涉猎儿童杂志的插图与配图，并在广告公司制作动画和电视广告脚本，广泛参与了各类绘画工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1963年与落语家结婚的濑名，以生孩子为契机开始制作幻灯片故事（纸芝居），并比绘本更早地以幻灯片故事《〇与□与△酱 相扑篇》作为作家出道。此后，她通过在孩子就读的幼儿园进行实演并反复修改，为了深化理论与实践，还参加了儿童文化研究所的幻灯片故事研究会等活动，直到2000年前后一直在持续发表幻灯片故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/cb79e4279c41f852ca70d64e3b88ed04-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "出自 彩色剪影透视幻灯片故事《雪的孩子》 濑名K子 画 1953年前后（上映：剪纸虫会）", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所谓“彩色剪影透视幻灯片故事”，是指利用身边的窗户或照明光线，透过使用彩色玻璃纸的剪影来营造梦幻般演出效果的幻灯片故事。濑名在日本银行工作期间，与学习研究社的年轻人共同创立了名为“剪纸虫会”的社团，并着手创作“彩色剪影透视幻灯片故事”。正是在这个时期，她被用玻璃纸制作的拼贴画所吸引，以此为契机，她开始采用拼贴画来创作绘本。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/c1afbf4162ab12ae0b90d81b40760587-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "左：《迎战狼的凯（出自〈冰雪女王〉）》　右：《女王与凯（出自〈冰雪女王〉）》皆为1955年　安徒生节第9回童画展参展作品", "1980年9月，濑名与出席国际安徒生奖颁奖典礼的赤羽末吉等人一同前往布拉格旅行，此后她也开始频繁出国。84年，她探访了少女时代起便爱读的《爱尔兰童话集》中“美人鱼神奇的壶（梅罗）”的故事发生地，并创作了绘本《梅罗》。海外之旅同样成为了孕育绘本构思的钻研契机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "text": "今でも大人気の『いやだいやだ』と『ねないこだれだ』は、せなさんのデビュー作「いやだいやだの絵本」シリーズ中の2作です。決してハッピーエンドではない結末なのに子どもの心を捉えて離さない魅力があり、作られてから50年以上たつにもかかわらず、絵柄も内容もまったく古びません。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "うさことおばけの、すっとぼけたやり取りが面白い『めがねうさぎ』。当時小学生だった息子さんにめがねが必要となったとき、楽しくめがねを使ってほしいとの思いから生まれた作品だそうです。せな作品のアイコンとも言えるおばけについては、せなさん自身の言葉が残っています。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「もちろんおばけは、怖いのよ。怖いけど、かわいい。怖いけど、見てみたい。大人になると、自分もおばけに会っていたことなんかすっかりわすれてしまうかもしれない。でも、子どもを見ていると、そういう気持ちがよくわかる。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "おばけや妖怪の魅力に取りつかれたせなさんは、「ゲゲゲの鬼太郎」の作者である水木しげるさんを訪ねるなど、妖怪の研究にも熱心に取り組み、『ばけものづかい』『ひとつめのくに』など、ユニークな妖怪の絵本もたくさん出しました。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "せなさんが絵本作家としてデビューしたのは1969年、37歳のときでした。作家としては遅咲きのデビューと言われますが、それ以前から幅広く絵に関わる仕事をし、熱心に研鑽を積んできました。本展では絵本の原画以外の作品も多く展示されており、せなさんの表現者としての一面を見ることができます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "幼い頃から本が好きだったせなさん。特に大きな影響を受けた本が最後のコーナーで紹介されています。ひとつは生涯の師となった武井武雄氏の本で、特に『おもちゃ箱』がお気に入りだったそうです。もうひとつは海外の子ども向け絵本『もじゃもじゃペーター』（ハインリヒ・ホフマン）で、お父さんから贈られたものをとても大切にしていました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "高校生の頃から画家の道を志すようになりましたが、厳しかったお母さんの反対により美術大学へ進むことをあきらめ、日本銀行へ就職することに。昼休みに出版社をまわってカットの持ち込みを続け、少女雑誌などに掲載されるようになりました。19歳のとき、童画家の武井武雄氏に師事。熱心に学びつつ、絵雑誌のカットや挿絵を手がけたり、広告代理店でアニメーションやCMコンテを制作するなど、幅広く絵の仕事にたずさわりました。"}, "「色影絵透視紙芝居」とは、身近な窓や照明の光を色セロファンを使った影絵に透過させて幻想的な演出効果を作ることのできる紙芝居です。せなさんは、日本銀行に勤めていた時期に、学習研究社の若い人たちと「かみきり虫の会」というサークルを立ち上げ「色影絵透視紙芝居」を手掛けました。このときにセロファンで作る貼り絵に魅力を感じたことがきっかけとなり、貼り絵で絵本を制作するようになります。"}, article_text:
絵本『ねないこだれだ』『めがねうさぎ』などで広く知られる絵本作家のせなけいこさん。おばけや妖怪、うさぎなどをモチーフにした絵本は時代を超えて読みつがれ、親子2代にわたってお世話になったという方も多くいらっしゃるのではないでしょうか。50年近くにわたるせなさんの画業をおよそ400点にのぼる原画や資料で紹介する「せなけいこ展」が刈谷市美術館（愛知県）で開催されています。

刈谷では7年ぶり2回目のせなけいこ展

刈谷市美術館では、2019年にも「せなけいこ展」が開催されました。その後、2024年にせなさんは逝去されましたが、今回は回顧展という意味もあり、前回よりもさらに充実した内容になりました。代表作の原画展示はもちろん、絵本作家としてデビューする前の仕事や、表現者としての活動にも注目し、豊富な資料と作品で「全仕事」を紹介します。

名作の原画がずらり

会場には「いやだいやだの絵本」シリーズや「あーんあんの絵本」シリーズなど、代表作の原画がずらり。懐かしい場面をたどるだけでなく、原画だからこそよくわかる、貼り絵の微妙なニュアンスや紙の質感を味わうことができます。

今でも大人気の『いやだいやだ』と『ねないこだれだ』は、せなさんのデビュー作「いやだいやだの絵本」シリーズ中の2作です。決してハッピーエンドではない結末なのに子どもの心を捉えて離さない魅力があり、作られてから50年以上たつにもかかわらず、絵柄も内容もまったく古びません。

うさことおばけの、すっとぼけたやり取りが面白い『めがねうさぎ』。当時小学生だった息子さんにめがねが必要となったとき、楽しくめがねを使ってほしいとの思いから生まれた作品だそうです。せな作品のアイコンとも言えるおばけについては、せなさん自身の言葉が残っています。

「もちろんおばけは、怖いのよ。怖いけど、かわいい。怖いけど、見てみたい。大人になると、自分もおばけに会っていたことなんかすっかりわすれてしまうかもしれない。でも、子どもを見ていると、そういう気持ちがよくわかる。」

おばけや妖怪の魅力に取りつかれたせなさんは、「ゲゲゲの鬼太郎」の作者である水木しげるさんを訪ねるなど、妖怪の研究にも熱心に取り組み、『ばけものづかい』『ひとつめのくに』など、ユニークな妖怪の絵本もたくさん出しました。

せなさんの絵本によく登場する「ルルちゃん」は、「私も小さい頃はこんなふうだった！」と共感してしまうほどリアルで生き生きとした女の子。長女の黒田かおるさんがモデルで、小さい頃はお兄さんから「いい子にしていないとまた絵本に描かれちゃいますよ」と言われていたそうです。現在はかおるさんも絵本作家として活動され、本展には監修者として関わっています。

「あの絵本ができるまで」

せなさんは、貼り絵で作品を制作しましたが、出版社へ持ち込む時にはダミー絵本という手製の絵本を作成していました。さらにその前の段階として絵コンテのような形での下書きも描いています。制作にかかわる膨大な資料も見どころのひとつです。

表現者・せなけいこ

せなさんが絵本作家としてデビューしたのは1969年、37歳のときでした。作家としては遅咲きのデビューと言われますが、それ以前から幅広く絵に関わる仕事をし、熱心に研鑽を積んできました。本展では絵本の原画以外の作品も多く展示されており、せなさんの表現者としての一面を見ることができます。

幼い頃から本が好きだったせなさん。特に大きな影響を受けた本が最後のコーナーで紹介されています。ひとつは生涯の師となった武井武雄氏の本で、特に『おもちゃ箱』がお気に入りだったそうです。もうひとつは海外の子ども向け絵本『もじゃもじゃペーター』（ハインリヒ・ホフマン）で、お父さんから贈られたものをとても大切にしていました。

高校生の頃から画家の道を志すようになりましたが、厳しかったお母さんの反対により美術大学へ進むことをあきらめ、日本銀行へ就職することに。昼休みに出版社をまわってカットの持ち込みを続け、少女雑誌などに掲載されるようになりました。19歳のとき、童画家の武井武雄氏に師事。熱心に学びつつ、絵雑誌のカットや挿絵を手がけたり、広告代理店でアニメーションやCMコンテを制作するなど、幅広く絵の仕事にたずさわりました。

1963年に落語家と結婚したせなさんは、出産を機に紙芝居の制作を始め、絵本よりも先に紙芝居『〇と□と△ちゃん おすもうのまき』で作家デビューを果たしました。その後、お子さんが通っている保育園で実演しては手直しをしたり、理論と実践を深めるため、子どもの文化研究所での紙芝居研究会に参加するなどして、2000年ごろまで継続的に紙芝居を発表しつづけました。

「色影絵透視紙芝居」とは、身近な窓や照明の光を色セロファンを使った影絵に透過させて幻想的な演出効果を作ることのできる紙芝居です。せなさんは、日本銀行に勤めていた時期に、学習研究社の若い人たちと「かみきり虫の会」というサークルを立ち上げ「色影絵透視紙芝居」を手掛けました。このときにセロファンで作る貼り絵に魅力を感じたことがきっかけとなり、貼り絵で絵本を制作するようになります。

せなさんは師である武井武雄氏らが立ち上げた日本童画会へ加入し、会が発足した1955年から解散した1961年まで熱心に童画展へ作品を出し続けました。ほかにも日本児童出版美術家連盟（童美連）に籍を置いたり「童画ぐるーぷ車」の展覧会へ初期から加わるなどして、表現の幅を大きく広げていきました。

1980年9月に国際アンデルセン賞授賞式に出席する赤羽末吉さんらとプラハまで旅をしたせなさんは、以降もたびたび海外に出かけるようになりました。84年には、少女時代からの愛読書『アイルランド童話集』にあった「人魚のふしぎな壺(メロウ)」の舞台を訪れ、絵本『メロウ』を制作しました。海外への旅もまた、絵本のアイデアを生み出す研鑽の場となりました。

戦前生まれのせなさんには、疎開の経験があります。当時のことを決して多くは語っていませんが、戦争という出来事は心に深く刻まれたことでしょう。1982年8月号の『日本児童文学』(日本児童文学者協会編)では絵本ストーリィ「お日さまとお月さまのけんか」が発表されました。当時は絵のない物語でしたが、それから20年近くたった2003年に、不安定な世界情勢を危ぶむ彼女の強い希望により、絵本『おひさまとおつきさまのけんか』となりました。

子どもとまっすぐに向き合い、真摯に創作の世界で努力を重ねた「表現者・せなけいこ」の姿は、日々、子どもたちと向き合う人や、創作の世界に関わっている人、そして関わろうとしている人たちに力を与えてくれるのではないでしょうか。 (ライター・岩田なおみ)

article_text:
VENUS ALFA è un viaggio nel sottosopra della cultura visiva tra storie kinky, glitch culturali e cattive ragazze che sfidano gli stereotipi, hackerano il gender gap e amplificano il female empowerment.

E se vi dicessi che per secoli mettere il rosa a una bambina sarebbe stato considerato strano, se non del tutto sbagliato?

Se oggi colleghiamo automaticamente il rosa alla femminilità e l’azzurro alla mascolinità, non è perché questi colori abbiano avuto da sempre un significato di genere. È il risultato di una delle operazioni di marketing meglio riuscite della storia. Come racconta la storica Jo B. Paoletti , autrice di Pink and Blue: Telling the Boys from the Girls in America , per molto tempo il rosa non fu associato a un determinato sesso. Nel Settecento era normale vedere aristocratici e sovrani sfoggiare completi di seta rosati, senza che questo mettesse in discussione la loro “virilità”.

La vera curiosità arriva all’inizio del Novecento: nel 1918 la rivista commerciale Earnshaw’s sosteneva che questa tonalità fosse più adatta ai maschi, vista la parentela con il rosso, colore forte e legato alla guerra, mentre l’azzurro, considerato più delicato e associato alla Vergine Maria, sarebbe stato indicato per le bambine. Ma non esisteva una regola universale. Negli anni Venti, infatti, alcuni grandi magazzini americani consigliavano ancora il rosa ai maschi e altri colori alle femmine. La distinzione che oggi ci sembra naturale si sarebbe affermata soprattutto nel secondo dopoguerra, fino a diventare un potentissimo strumento commerciale. Il colore, insomma, non è nato femminile, ci è diventato.

Ed è proprio quando comincia a trasformarsi in un codice commerciale che alcune artiste e stiliste iniziano a manipolarlo, rovesciarlo e restituirgli una nuova forza. La prima grande scossa arriva nel 1937 con Elsa Schiaparelli , che lancia il celebre Shocking Pink , una tonalità intensa, artificiale e volutamente provocatoria, destinata a diventare la firma della maison. Non è più necessariamente delicato o rassicurante, può essere teatrale, eccentrico, scandaloso.

Nel 1953 Marilyn Monroe lo rende poi iconico al cinema in Gli uomini preferiscono le bionde , indossando il celebre abito confetto disegnato da William Travilla durante Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend (ripreso anche da Madonna nel video di Material Girl ). Pochi anni dopo, nel 1959, ci pensa Barbie con l’esercito di plastica della Mattel a colonizzare l’immaginario planetario, trasformando il rosa in un impero totalizzante da cui nessuna bambina (e nessuna epoca) sarebbe più uscita indenne.

E cosa combinano le artiste con tutto questo pigmento così trionfalmente “di genere”? Semplice, lo sequestrano e lo capovolgono, trasformandolo in un’arma di guerriglia visiva. Louise Bourgeois lo cuce addosso a sculture e tessuti carnosi, esplorando la vulnerabilità con ago, filo e brividi, mentre Pipilotti Rist lo fa esplodere in installazioni video immersive che ti avvolgono come una nebbia allucinogena al gusto di fragola. Un’ossessione che Portia Munson spinge fino al lato più morboso del quotidiano con Pink Project: Table, dove migliaia di cianfrusaglie rosa – giocattoli, trucchi, sex toys – compongono un catalogo grottesco di ciò che il mercato ha stabilito che una donna dovrebbe desiderare. La femminilità rassicurante si trasforma così in un’inquietante claustrofobia commerciale.

E poi arriva lei. Kitten Kay Sera , attrice e icona californiana che si è autoproclamata «la persona più rosa del pianeta». Dagli anni Ottanta indossa esclusivamente abiti di questa tinta, vive in una casa delle bambole a Hollywood e ha trasformato questa passione in un vero e proprio manifesto identitario. Qui il meccanismo si ribalta: ciò che l’industria aveva imposto dall’esterno diventa improvvisamente uno strumento di radicale autoritratto. Il marketing esulta, il femminismo interroga i suoi testi sacri, ma lei, nel dubbio, tinge il suo cagnolino di rosa. Rosa truffatore.

«Pink, it’s my new obsession / Pink, it’s not even a question». (Aerosmith)

article_text:
Lubov , a closely watched gallery in New York’s Chinatown neighborhood, will remain open after the death of its founder Francisco Correa Cordero earlier this year.

Cordero, who died at 37 in August , founded Lubov in 2016 and exhibited artists such as Eunnam Hong, My Barbarian, Andres Serrano, Mimi Park, Shannon Cartier Lucy, and Covey Gong. The gallery was named after Luba Drozd, to whom Cordero was married when he first opened the space.

On Tuesday, the gallery announced that it would continue under the leadership of Mode Bonafilia and Kristen Wasik . Bonafilia had already been with the gallery, serving as its director of community programming and education since 2025. Wasik had been a director at the gallery between 2023 and 2024, and returned to Lubov earlier this year, having previously worked at Chart and the now-defunct Lyles & King .

“Following Cordero’s sudden passing in August, Bonafilia and Wasik committed without hesitation to carrying the gallery forward,” the gallery wrote in a statement posted to Instagram . “At a time in which alternative spaces in New York are becoming increasingly scarce, they regard Lubov’s continuation as essential. Whether or not to continue the gallery was never a question. Under their direction, the gallery will honor Cordero’s legacy while building upon it, supporting artists who make work out of necessity rather than for market value.”

Lubov’s first exhibition under the gallery’s new ownership will be a solo show for Michael Hafftka, a New York–based painter. His exhibition opens there on October 24.

article_text:
Films and events

Galas

Tender Loving Care

In a world that feels increasingly untethered from human connection, the incomparable Mike Leigh returns with a thought-provoking and compassionate view of urban life.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Mike Leigh

With Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson

UK 2026. 107min

Courtesy of STUDIOCANAL

Language English

Access information

Thursday 15 October 18:00

Audio description

Closed Captions (CC) via WatchWord smart glasses

Saturday 17 October 12:15

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Sunday 18 October 13:05

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

In contemporary London, social workers Amy and Rosie navigate the stressors and joys of life together, be that work, family or messy dating lives. Leigh and his tight ensemble – Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Kate O’Flynn, Alice Bailey Johnson – breathe life into these characters with a deep naturalism that illuminates life’s complexities with warmth, humour and much-needed kindness.

Kristy Matheson

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Ink

Danny Boyle brings a seismic moment in Rupert Murdoch’s Fleet Street career blazingly to life, employing the breathtaking style of a story torn from the headlines.

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning

In Clio Barnard’s poignant drama, five childhood friends from Birmingham find their lifelong bonds tested as adulthood brings fractured relationships, unfulfilled dreams and long-buried secrets to light.

In the Shadows

Jasmine Jobson leads a brilliant ensemble in bringing the inspirational story of champion East End boxer Ramla Ali to the screen.

title_original: ‘La Bola Negra’ Earns $277,500 in Limited Release as Netflix Reports Box Office Results for the First Time in History
editorial_title_zh: 《黑球》（La Bola Negra）在限定上映中斩获277,500美元，Netflix有史以来首次公布票房成绩
editorial_excerpt_zh: 欢迎来到激动人心的票房报道世界，泰德·萨兰多斯（Ted Sarandos）！
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "被视为奥斯卡热门竞争者的宏大历史史诗片《黑球》（La Bola Negra）于本周末在少数影院限定上映。该片的票房表现强劲，仅在纽约和洛杉矶的4家影院上映便斩获277,500美元，单馆平均票房高达69,375美元。这是有史以来非英语电影第二高的单馆平均票房。但更重要的是，该片也创造了历史，成为Netflix首部公开披露票房收入的发行作品。", "links": [{"text": "La Bola Negra", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/la-bola-negra/"}, {"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Netflix", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/netflix/"}, {"text": "box office", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/box-office/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这标志着这家流媒体巨头战略的转变。此前，该公司为了符合奥斯卡参评资格，将电影独家在院线公映数周，但对实际票房收入一直讳莫如深。它曾短暂透露过《玻璃洋葱：利刃出鞘》（Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery）的票房成绩，但从未官方正式公布。不过，这对Netflix来说是一个全新的黎明、全新的一天，它将开始像其同行制片厂和流媒体同行一样报告票房成绩。", "links": [{"text": "pulled back the curtain", "url": "https://variety.com/2022/film/box-office/glass-onion-box-office-netflix-knives-out-1235443658/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_A1332_e4d22d.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "梅丽莎·耶鲁（Melissa Yerou）、杰米·金（Jamie King）、特雷西·罗森布卢姆（Tracy Rosenblum）和克里斯蒂安·齐尔科（Christian Zilko）于2026年10月17日在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶 Lumen 举办的 IndieWire 电影制作未来峰会上。", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/UFP25_R02_104y_v04.189840.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "克利夫·布思的进一步冒险。布拉德·皮特饰演克利夫·布思。图片来源：Netflix © 2026", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，准备好迎接关于大卫·芬奇（David Fincher）的《克利夫·布思的进一步冒险》（The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth）、格蕾塔·葛韦格（Greta Gerwig）的《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》（Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew）、塔伊加·维迪提（Taika Waititi）的动画长片《查理与巧克力工厂》（Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory）、彼得·博格（Peter Berg）的《蚊子碗》（The Mosquito Bowl）以及丹尼·博伊尔（Danny Boyle）的《墨水》（Ink）在院线上映时表现如何的头条新闻吧。所有这些作品都将有大约一个月或更长时间的院线窗口期，这将使它们能够登陆更多银幕。但Netflix会喜欢这种聚光灯下的审视吗？苹果公司似乎对此深恶痛绝，他们发现有拿得出手的作品时（《F1》）去报道票房感觉很棒，而没有拿得出手作品时（《飞月情海》、《阿盖尔：神秘特工》）则没那么好受。", "links": [{"text": "theatrical windows", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/news/netflix-report-box-office-theatrical-releases-1236854834/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但Netflix目前面临着更大的问题。其股价正陷入低谷，并且刚刚实施了一轮严厉的裁员潮，解雇了1,000名员工，并让首席内容官贝拉·巴贾里亚（Bela Bajaria）离职，由福斯和迪士尼资深高管彼得·赖斯（Peter Rice）取而代之。拥抱传统的院线发行会为Netflix带来一笔无价的新收入来源，还是华尔街会在发现票房表现不佳时，将票房收入当作又一个痛击泰德·萨兰多斯的指标？", "links": [{"text": "jettisoning Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/business/netflix-bela-bajaria-out-chief-content-officer-1235222301/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "到目前为止，Netflix似乎对这些结果感到满意。该流媒体平台指出，《黑球》对同性恋历史的审视吸引了年轻观众，这正是推动票房反弹的同一群人。为此，其首周末观众中有51%在35岁以下，其中25至34岁之间的购票者占比最大，达到39%。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《黑球》是Netflix在戛纳以约500万美元买下的，它可能在另一个关键方面非常重要。奖项评委似乎正在接受它，它有机会战胜《奥德赛》（The Odyssey），为Netflix赢得它长期以来梦寐以求的奥斯卡最佳影片奖。这种认可的价值远超这部历史史诗在票房上赚到的任何收入。", "links": [{"text": "seem to be embracing it", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/industry/hollywood-soften-netflix-best-picture-oscars-la-bola-negra-1235221518/"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“ La Bola Negra ,” a sprawling historical epic that is viewed as a major Oscar contender, opened in limited release this weekend. The film ‘s grosses were strong, with “La Bola Negra” earning $277,500 from just four venues in New York and Los Angeles, for a per-screen average of $69,375. It’s the second-highest per-screen average for a Non-English language film of all time. article_text:
“ La Bola Negra ,” a sprawling historical epic that is viewed as a major Oscar contender, opened in limited release this weekend. The film ‘s grosses were strong, with “La Bola Negra” earning $277,500 from just four venues in New York and Los Angeles, for a per-screen average of $69,375. It’s the second-highest per-screen average for a Non-English language film of all time. But more importantly the film also makes history, becoming the first Netflix release to ever publicly disclose box office grosses.

That marks a shift in strategy for the streamer, which has released films in theaters exclusively for several weeks to qualify for Oscars, but has been dodgy about the money they’re actually making. It briefly pulled back the curtain on the results for “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery,” but never officially. But it’s a new dawn, it’s a new day for Netflix, which will start to report box office results like the rest of its studio and streaming brethren.

So get ready for headlines about how David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” Taika Waititi’s animated feature “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory,” Peter Berg’s “The Mosquito Bowl,” and Danny Boyle’s “Ink” fare when they open in theaters. All will have theatrical windows of roughly a month or more, which will give them access to more screens. But will Netflix enjoy the scrutiny? Apple sure seemed to hate it, discovering it was great to report box office when you had the goods (“F1”) and not so hot when you did not (“Fly Me to the Moon,” “Argylle”).

But Netflix has bigger problems at the moment. Its stock is in a rut and it has just enacted a punishing wave of layoffs, pink-slipping 1,000 employees and jettisoning Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria in favor of Fox and Disney vet Peter Rice. Will an embrace of traditional theatrical releases provide Netflix with an invaluable new source of revenue or will Wall Street treat box office grosses as another metric to pummel Ted Sarandos with when it finds them lacking?

So far, Netflix seems happy with the results. The streamer noted that “La Bola Negra’s” look at gay history appealed to younger audiences, the same ones driving the box office rebound. To that end, 51% of its opening weekend crowd was under the age of 35, with ticket buyers between 25 to 34 making up the largest age group at 39%.

“La Bola Negra,” which Netflix picked up at Cannes for around $5 million, may be important in another key way. Awards voters seem to be embracing it and there’s a chance that it could overcome “The Odyssey” to land Netflix the Best Picture Oscar it has long coveted. That kind of validation would be worth a lot more than whatever the historical epic earns at the box office.

editorial_title_zh: 问答：维维安·埃斯德尔（Viviane Esders），卡罗尔·施密茨（Carole Schmitz）访谈
editorial_excerpt_zh: 维维安·埃斯德尔：收藏就是构建一段记忆。有些收藏家积累作品，而另一些人则近乎不由自主地构建了一个故事。维维安 […] Cet article The Questionnaire : Viviane Esders by Carole Schmitz est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "维维安·埃斯德尔：收藏就是构建一段记忆", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有些收藏家积累作品，而另一些人则近乎不由自主地构建了一个故事。维维安·埃斯德尔（Viviane Esders）便属于后一类。她的职业生涯既不能简化为对大约2,500张摄影作品的收藏，也不能简化为画廊经营者和专家的履历：它跨越了当代摄影史上的几个决定性时刻，并在这一过程中展现了摄影地位本身的转变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当她在1979年于巴黎开设画廊时，摄影尚未在当代艺术世界中占据几十年后那样的地位。它既不是博物馆里的普遍存在，也未真正建立在艺术市场的运作机制之中。然而，维维安·埃斯德尔却选择将其作为自己的领地。在蓬皮杜中心对面，她展出了如今被视为重要人物的艺术家的作品，从威廉·埃格尔斯顿（William Eggleston）到路易吉·吉里（Luigi Ghirri），从加布里埃莱·巴西利科（Gabriele Basilico）到莉塞特·莫多尔（Lisette Model），还有一些更具独特性、有时难以归入该媒介线性历史的实践。这种选择已经透露出她的某种观察方式：收藏或推崇摄影并不一定意味着去识别稳妥的投资对象，而是在其成为不证自明的事实之前识别出一种张力。她作为专家的工作始于1990年代初，这再次改变了她的视角。画廊之后是市场；发现之后是评估；观察之后是价值问题。近三十年来，她检视作品、为收藏家提供咨询并组织拍卖。通过这些，她获得了关于摄影作品流通的几乎实实在在的知识：它们的出处、品相、珍稀程度，以及是什么让一张照片成为、或未能成为注定流传下去的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这段经历本可以引导她建立一个根据市场既定准则构建的理性收藏，但她没有。她的个人收藏与其说是出于某种论证，不如说是受偶遇的驱使。它汇集了各种截然不同的摄影作品：肖像、风景、建筑、城市景观、工业、观念实验。将它们连接在一起的未必是共同的美学，而是它们抓住视线的能力。也许这正是其真正意义所在。收藏从来不只是图像的堆砌。它是一种蒙太奇的形式。它创造了在孤立作品中并不存在的联系、摩擦和呼应。在维维安·埃斯德尔的收藏中，这种蒙太奇逐渐构成了一部摄影的主观历史：一部由发现、忠诚、友谊、好奇心和信念交织而成的历史。2022年维维安·埃斯德尔奖（Viviane Esders Prize）的创立延续了这一逻辑。奖励60岁以上的欧洲摄影师意味着将主流目光从当代创作中移开。在市场往往青睐新鲜事物的当下，她选择了时间的深度。她对发现的兴奋过去后留下的东西感兴趣，当一个创作主体已经有时间成形、分枝、有时甚至留在阴影中时，她依然关注。这一举动绝非偶然。它提出了一个根本问题：为什么有些作品成为了历史，而另一些作品却留在了叙事的边缘？又是谁决定了什么值得被保留？今天，随着她的收藏日益被构想为一个需要传承的创作主体，她的职业生涯似乎画上了一个完整的圆。她曾率先帮助摄影进入市场和体制认可的领域；如今，她发现自己面临着相反的问题：私人记忆如何才能融入集体历史？因此，收藏与其说是一项遗产，不如说是一个传承的载体。这些摄影作品不再仅仅是被拥有的物件。它们成为了一个时代的碎片，是当该媒介的地位发生变化时，对摄影的某种特定观看方式的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，对维维安·埃斯德尔而言，收藏与其说是紧抓不放，不如说是建立连接。连接艺术家、世代、实践、市场的历史以及观看的历史。最重要的是，保护官方历史总是面临被抹去的风险的东西：先于认可的直觉、留在边缘的作品，以及其价值无法立即通过可见度来衡量的摄影师。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，她的收藏可以被解读为一本没有自画像的自传。一部从某个特定立场讲述的摄影史，这个立场属于一个曾经注视过它、推崇过它、评估过它并最终选择它的人。因为到头来，收藏或许并非关于拥有图像。而是关于决定当它们的时代消逝之后，哪些图像仍能对我们诉说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Instagram: @vivianeesders", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您的第一次摄影启蒙？维维安·埃斯德尔：由于我不是摄影师，我作为青少年的第一次启蒙是萨姆·莱文（Sam Levin）拍摄的碧姬·芭铎（Brigitte Bardot）的照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您童年的一段摄影记忆？维维安·埃斯德尔：我父亲6岁时的肖像照，由ORA摄影师将其打扮成俄罗斯王子，摆放在我祖母的书房里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您童年使用的相机？维维安·埃斯德尔：柯达布朗尼闪光相机（Kodak Brownie Flash）。", true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您希望自己能拍下的一张照片：维维安·埃斯德尔：安塞尔·亚当斯（Ansel Adams）的《月升，新墨西哥州》（Moonrise, New Mexico）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最触动您的那张照片？维维安·埃斯德尔：理查德·阿维顿（Richard Avedon）拍摄的其垂死父亲雅各布·以色列·阿维顿（Jacob Israel Avedon）的九幅肖像组照，1969–1973年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有哪张照片曾让你感到愤怒？薇维安·埃斯德斯：面对一张照片，我不会感到愤怒。但我可能会感到焦虑、抗拒或震惊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哪张照片改变了世界？薇维安·埃斯德斯：尼谢福尔·涅普斯于1827年夏天拍摄的第一张照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "又是哪张照片改变了你的世界？薇维安·埃斯德斯：宇航员威廉·安德斯于1968年拍摄的《地出》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你个人精神殿堂中的一张关键照片？薇维安·埃斯德斯：黛安·阿勃丝的《手持国旗的爱国青年，纽约市》（Patriotic Young Man with a Flag. NYC.），1967年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一幅图像中，你最感兴趣的是什么？薇维安·埃斯德斯：它所讲述的故事，以及它所传达的情感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在面孔、风景或物体中，你最关注什么细节？薇维安·埃斯德斯：我热衷于肖像摄影，因此我的注意力主要被眼神所吸引。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃利奥特·厄维特曾说：“色彩是描述性的。黑白是诠释性的。”你赞同吗？薇维安·埃斯德斯：不完全赞同。对我而言，色彩并非描述性的。摄影师的个人视野能够表达出与黑白摄影同样丰富的诗意情感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一张照片能否比现实更真实？薇维安·埃斯德斯：是的，它确实可以比现实更真实，比如格雷戈里·克鲁德森或托马斯·德曼德的摆拍图像，又或是通过内在的戏剧张力来揭示隐形的事物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你看来，什么才算一张好照片？薇维安·埃斯德斯：说实话，什么是好照片？我没有客观的定义。标准会随着时期和风尚而演变。如今，一张“模糊”的照片也被认为是好照片。参见爱丽舍摄影博物馆（Photo Elysée）“模糊”展览的目录。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你看来，成为一名优秀的摄影师需要具备什么素质？薇维安·埃斯德斯：创造力，以及发展自己风格的耐心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你希望由谁来为你拍摄肖像？薇维安·埃斯德斯：我的祖父阿尔芒·埃斯德斯（Armand Esders），我从未见过他，但他是一位杰出的艺术赞助人。", "translated": true}, Facebook——为什么？薇维安·埃斯德斯：Facebook——上面有关于艺术、文学和历史的照片与文字。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自从社交媒体兴起以来，摄影发生了什么变化？薇维安·埃斯德斯：紧迫感这个概念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Viviane Esders : Collecting is building a memory

There are collectors who accumulate works, and others who, almost despite themselves, build a story. Viviane Esders belongs to the latter category. Her career cannot be reduced either to a collection of some 2,500 prints or to a career as a gallerist and expert: it spans several decisive moments in the history of contemporary photography and reveals, in the process, the transformation of photography’s status itself.

When she opened her Paris gallery in 1979, photography had not yet acquired the position it would occupy a few decades later within the contemporary art world. It was neither ubiquitous in museums nor truly established within the mechanisms of the art market. Yet Viviane Esders chose to make it her territory. Across from the Centre Pompidou, she exhibited artists who are now regarded as major figures, from William Eggleston to Luigi Ghirri, from Gabriele Basilico to Lisette Model, as well as more singular practices that were sometimes difficult to fit into a linear history of the medium. This choice already reveals something about her way of seeing: collecting or championing photography does not necessarily mean identifying safe bets but recognizing an intensity before it becomes self-evident. Her work as an expert, which began in the early 1990s, shifted her perspective once again. After the gallery came the market; after discovery, evaluation; after observation, the question of value. For nearly three decades, she examined works, advised collectors, and organized auctions. In doing so, she acquired an almost physical knowledge of the circulation of photographs: their provenance, condition, rarity, but also what makes a print become, or fail to become, a work destined to survive.

This experience could have led to a rational collection, constructed according to the established canons of the market. It did not. Her personal collection is driven more by encounters than by demonstration. It brings together photographs of very different kinds: portraits, landscapes, architecture, urban scenes, industry, conceptual experiments. What connects them is not necessarily a shared aesthetic, but their ability to hold the gaze. Perhaps this is where its true significance lies. A collection is never simply an accumulation of images. It is a form of montage. It creates connections, frictions and correspondences that did not exist within the isolated work. In Viviane Esders’s collection, this montage gradually composes a subjective history of photography: a history made of discoveries, loyalties, friendships, curiosities and convictions. The creation of the Viviane Esders Prize in 2022 extended this logic. Rewarding European photographers over the age of sixty means shifting the dominant gaze from contemporary creation. Where the market often favors novelty, she chooses the depth of time. She is interested in what remains once the excitement of discovery has passed, when a body of work has had time to take shape, to branch out, and sometimes to remain in the shadows. This gesture is far from incidental. It raises a fundamental question: why do some works become historical while others remain on the margins of the narrative? And who decides what deserves to be preserved? Today, as her collection is increasingly conceived as a body of work to be passed on, her career seems to describe a full circle. She first helped photography enter the realms of the market and institutional recognition; she now finds herself confronted with the opposite question: how can a private memory become part of a collective history? The collection thus becomes less a heritage than a vehicle for transmission. The prints are no longer merely objects that are owned. They become fragments of an era, traces of a particular way of looking at photography at the precise moment when the medium was changing status.

For Viviane Esders, collecting is therefore not so much about holding on as it is about connecting. Connecting artists, generations, practices, histories of the market and histories of looking. And, above all, preserving what official history always risks erasing: the intuitions that precede recognition, the works that remain on the margins, the photographers whose value cannot immediately be measured by their visibility.

Her collection can thus be read as an autobiography without a self-portrait. A history of photography told from the singular position of someone who has looked at it, championed it, evaluated it and ultimately chosen it. Because, in the end, collecting may not be about possessing images. It is about deciding which ones will still have something to say to us once their era has disappeared.

Your first photographic revelation ? Viviane Esders: As I am not a photographer, my first revelation as a teenager was a photograph of Brigitte Bardot by Sam Levin.

A photographic memory from your childhood? Viviane Esders: A portrait of my father at the age of six, dressed up as a Russian prince by the ORA photographer, displayed in my grandmother’s library.

The camera of your childhood? Viviane Esders: A Kodak Brownie Flash.

The one you use today? Viviane Esders: I use my phone to capture my memories.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Viviane Esders: Sabine Weiss.

The image you wish you had taken Viviane Esders: Moonrise, New Mexico by Ansel Adams.

The one that moved you the most? Viviane Esders: Richard Avedon’s series of nine portraits of his dying father, Jacob Israel Avedon , 1969–1973.

And the one that made you angry? Viviane Esders: I cannot become angry in front of a photograph. But I can feel anguish, repulsion or shock.

Which photograph changed the world? Viviane Esders: The first photograph made by Nicéphore Niépce in the summer of 1827.

And which photograph changed your world? Viviane Esders: Earthrise , taken by astronaut William Anders in 1968.

A key image in your personal pantheon? Viviane Esders: Diane Arbus, Patriotic Young Man with a Flag. NYC. , 1967.

What interests you most in an image? Viviane Esders: The story it tells, together with the emotion it conveys.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape or an object? Viviane Esders: I am passionate about portraiture, so my attention is primarily drawn to the gaze.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? Viviane Esders: Not entirely. For me, color is not descriptive. The photographer’s personal vision can express just as much poetic emotion as black and white.

In your view, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Viviane Esders: The most perfect technique is useless if there is no emotion. An image is above all connected to the photographer’s culture, experience and sensitivity.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? Viviane Esders: The criteria of beauty are constantly evolving and differ from one culture to another, extending far beyond aesthetics. For me, beauty also describes that which is worthy of universal admiration.

What elements can make silence visible in a photograph? Viviane Esders: An empty space, a solitary subject, an atmosphere.

Can a photograph be truer than reality? Viviane Esders: Yes, it can be truer than reality, in staged images such as those by Gregory Crewdson or Thomas Demand, or by revealing the invisible through an inner dramatic intensity.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? Viviane Esders: Absolutely. It all depends on the photographer’s message. It can also be used to manipulate, for propaganda or disinformation.

What, in your opinion, makes a good photograph? Viviane Esders: In fact, what is a good photograph? I have no objective definition. Criteria evolve according to periods and fashions. Today, a “blurred” photograph is considered good. See the catalogue of the Blur exhibition at Photo Elysée.

In your opinion, what quality is necessary to become a good photographer? Viviane Esders: Creativity and patience in developing your own style.

The person you would like to be photographed by? Viviane Esders: My grandfather Armand Esders, whom I never knew but who was an exceptional patron of the arts.

An essential photography book? Viviane Esders: The Larousse Dictionary of World Photography , to which I contributed.

What is the last photograph you took? Viviane Esders: An installation by Richard Long at the Château de Rochechouart.

On social media, are you more Instagram or Facebook—and why? Viviane Esders: Facebook—photos and texts about art, literature and history.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? Viviane Esders: The notion of urgency.

What is your view of AI? Viviane Esders: I think AI is an essential tool, with its limitations.

Color or black and white? Viviane Esders: Both. Why oppose them?

Natural light or artificial light? Viviane Esders: Difficult to choose between them, because both have their uses depending on the choice of image and its spirit.

Which city seems the most photogenic to you? Viviane Esders: New York—it is my second “homeland.” But photogenic qualities can be found everywhere, even in the most ordinary cities, such as Savannakhet.

The city, country or culture you dream of discovering? Viviane Esders: The Vanuatu Islands. I once offered for auction some magnificent nineteenth-century photographic albums documenting the landscapes and customs there, which still make me dream.

The place you never tire of? Viviane Esders: The Hôtel Drouot in Paris.

The image that represents, for you, the current state of the world? Viviane Esders: The collapse of the World Trade Center towers in 2001.

Your favorite drug? Viviane Esders: None.

Your best way to disconnect? Viviane Esders: A nap.

Your latest extravagance? Viviane Esders: Learning to play the kora, a 21-string lute.

Your greatest professional extravagance? Viviane Esders: My solo trip to Russia in 1990, during a year of widespread shortages, to meet Russian photographers with the view of organizing an exhibition, without speaking a single word of Russian.

The profession you would never have wanted to pursue? Viviane Esders: To be in the military.

The last thing you did for the first time? Viviane Esders: Eat snails.

Your greatest regret? Viviane Esders: Not speaking Russian.

If you had to start all over again? Viviane Esders: I would do exactly the same thing.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be at the table? Viviane Esders: Julian Levy, the organizer of the first photography exhibition in New York in 1931.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? Viviane Esders: They can say whatever they want…

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? Viviane Esders: That I am a determined and combative woman, something I try to express in my memoirs, which I am currently writing.

One last word? Viviane Esders: Thank you, photographers.

article_text:
Kartik Aaryan ’s upcoming action drama “ Captain India ” is set amid the Houthi conflict in Yemen, Variety understands.

The film marks Aaryan’s first turn as a pilot. Shimit Amin directs the project, which is based on a real humanitarian evacuation. Aaryan’s character leads the rescue effort.

That conflict is central to the story and adds a geopolitical dimension to the drama. How exactly the fighting figures in the plot has not been disclosed. The film is expected to follow the obstacles of carrying out a humanitarian mission as tensions rise.

Olivia Wilde Eyes Oscars History With 'The Invite' as the First Woman to Direct Herself to an Acting Nomination

Pedro Pascal in 'Behemoth!': The Oscar-Worthy Role That He (and Latinos) Have Been Waiting For

The Saudi-Houthi confrontation that continues today dates to 2015, when Houthi forces took the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and Saudi Arabia began a military campaign. Variety understands that “Captain India” draws on what was among the hardest rescue operations India has carried out, in Yemen that same year, when the country evacuated its own citizens along with people from around the world.

Popular on Variety

T-Series and Baweja Studios produce “Captain India” in association with Dopamine Studios, Aaryan’s banner. Bhushan Kumar of T-Series is among the producers, and S B Films handles production. Nash Vazifdar, Sanchit Gupta and Priyadarshee Shrivastava wrote the screenplay.

Amin, meanwhile, is best known for directing “Chak De! India” and “Rocket Singh: Salesman of the Year” (2009), both for Yash Raj Films, and has largely stayed away from feature directing in the years since. article_text:
Black Bear has acquired the rights to a comedy spec script from up-and-coming writing duo Cassidy Alla and Read Masino, Variety can reveal exclusively

According to an official logline, the untitled film “tells the story of when a mother and daughter inadvertently start dating the same man; the whole family – each at their own crossroad in life and love – must deal with the chaotic fallout.”

Related Stories

Jamie Dornan Says There's 'Pressure' to Taking Over Aragorn Role in 'Lord of the Rings: Hunt for Gollum': I'm Not 'Trying to Outdo' Viggo Mortensen

Director Gregory Nava Remembers Dolores Huerta, the Civil Rights Icon Who Introduced Him to His Wife and Trusted Them With Her Life Story

Alla and Masino, both working toward their feature breakouts, have a movie in development at Netflix with Berlanti/Schechter producing and Nahnatchka Khan (“Totally Killer”) directing. The duo met while working as assistants at Apatow Productions. Masino worked as a writers’ assistant on Amazon’s “Spider-Noir” and Apple’s “Brothers” and “The Muppet Show,” while Alla worked for showrunner Justin Noble, co-creator of “The Sex Lives of College Girls.”

“This script is one of the funniest and most poignant scripts we have seen in years about romance, family and the dysfunction so often associated with both,” said Michael Heimler, Partner, President of Production & Operations at Black Bear. “Cassidy and Read are two of the most exciting voices we’ve read in some time, and we can’t wait to bring this story to life.”

Alla and Masino added in a joint statement, “We had so much fun writing this chaotic comedy about a family (not to be confused with a family comedy) and couldn’t ask for a better partner on this project than Black Bear.”

Black Bear, which launched its distribution arm in 2025, is the studio behind recent films like “Train Dreams,” “Sing Sing” and “The Imitation Game.” The upcoming Black Bear slate includes “Honeymoon / Funeral,” starring Rebecca Ferguson, Greta Lee and Carrie Coon; “Wicker,” starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage; and Guy Ritchie’s “Wife and Dog” with Benedict Cumberbatch and Rosamund Pike.

Alla is represented by UTA and Mosaic. Masino is represented by UTA and Artists First.

article_text:
Announcement

MassArt Graduate Assistantships Provide Hands-On Experience to Launch Your Career

MassArt’s Graduate Assistantships support students’ interests and professional development beyond graduation.

MassArt Graduate programs structure robust assistantship offerings each semester for its graduate student population. The assistantships are paid opportunities that build professional and academic experience while supporting teaching, research, studios, galleries, and administration. Intended to be more than jobs, they provide mentorship and wider connection to the college, outside of a student’s specific grad program.

Current student, Lucy Bennett (MFA Studio Arts ‘27), describes their assistantships as “such an important extension of my MFA experience. Through my teaching assistantships, I’ve been able to work alongside faculty and undergraduate students and see how different artists approach making, problem-solving, and learning. Teaching has become another way of learning for me.”

The graduate assistantships are organized into two categories: teaching and technical, with the latter generating a broad range of possibilities: Everything from skill-building in one of MassArt’s studio facilities — for example, ceramics, digital fabrication, printing, and more — to work that centers cultural change in the Justice Equity & Transformation office or social media management and design in Marketing.

Bennet’s second assistantship (students may have up to two each semester) is in MassArt’s Graduate gallery, MassArt x SoWa .

“Working at the gallery has been one of the absolute highlights of my graduate experience. I love working First Fridays, meeting artists, helping with installations and de-installations, and getting to participate in the curatorial side of the gallery through experiences like jurying exhibitions. I’ve also been able to build relationships with artists, staff and faculty, and people working in other galleries in the area. It has given me the kind of involvement and hands-on experience in the arts community that I had been wanting so badly, and it has been incredibly enriching!”

Hands-on experience is precisely what the assistantships are all about, giving students something concrete to launch from as they seek employment in their chosen fields or are applying to other competitive opportunities.

Fall 2027 applications are now open for all the MFA programs at the Massachusetts College of Art and Design (MassArt) in Boston.

article_text:
Si terrà dal 21 gennaio al 13 giugno 2027, nell’omonimo emirato, la 17 a edizione della Biennale di Sharjah , organizzata dalla Sharjah Art Foundation e intitolata What Remains Sits Restive . Curata da Angela Harutyunyan e Paula Nascimento , la Biennale riunisce 109 artisti provenienti da Africa, America Latina, Europa orientale e Medio Oriente e indaga come il nostro presente sia turbato da ciò che resta di un passato non vissuto, dai progetti sconfitti ma ancora vivi di una modernità fondata sull’emancipazione universale. Nell’intervista di anteprima, le curatrici anticipano cosa vedremo e il loro rapporto con l’emirato.

Come è nato il concetto della Biennale 2027?

Paula Nascimento: «Il concetto è stato definito attraverso conversazioni con gli artisti – sia la mia che la loro esperienza con Sharjah e le sue infrastrutture fisiche; così come una serie di domande emerse non solo in queste conversazioni, ma soprattutto riflettendo sul mondo in cui viviamo oggi. Le storie e i cicli di violenza persistono e ritornano, e come queste storie persistono non come ripetizione, ma come sedimenti e processi mutati che rimangono attivi nel presente. In questo senso, la proposta di pensare alle infrastrutture come a un metodo racchiude sia la forma costruita e le risposte ai siti e alle architetture di Sharjah, sia espande la riflessione in modi intangibili, sui sistemi, le circolazioni, le relazioni interspecie, ecc.

In tal senso, che tipo di spazi creano e abitano gli “artisti” attraverso le loro pratiche simboliche? Quali sono questi spazi di possibilità, o quali possibilità offrono che possono unirci? Inoltre, intendo la biennale anche come un processo collaborativo e generativo di condivisione e scambio di idee, come un dialogo continuo che ci permette di speculare insieme. Sebbene io e Angela abbiamo adottato approcci, geografie e artisti diversi, c’è una conversazione in corso, e tendo a pensare alle due mostre quasi come a una danza; a volte si completano a vicenda, altre volte si allontanano, ma sempre in dialogo».

Come hai selezionato gli artisti? Quali elementi della loro pratica ti hanno “spinto” a sceglierli?

Paula Nascimento: «La mia selezione è avvenuta in diverse fasi, ma la maggior parte del lavoro degli artisti selezionati risponde direttamente, o talvolta tangenzialmente, al concetto della Biennale e agli spunti che ho inizialmente condiviso con loro: sia l’invito a pensare o a riformulare le proprie idee in termini di concetto di infrastruttura, sia l’interesse per pratiche che integrano una prassi pedagogica, senza essere didattiche. Ci sono artisti con cui collaboro da tempo, e quindi si tratta di una continuazione di conversazioni che abbiamo avuto nel corso del tempo e di diversi progetti, e ci sono artisti con cui collaboro per la prima volta.

C’è anche un’enfasi su alcune aree geografiche da cui provengo, in particolare l’Africa lusofona e le sue diaspore allargate. Tuttavia, la geografia non limita affatto la selezione, ma direi che riflette anche una rete di relazioni e spazi che mi interessano. Oltre agli artisti che hanno risposto a queste domande, ho incluso artisti con pratiche interdisciplinari, un mix di artisti storici e artisti contemporanei, e artisti che realizzano nuove opere su commissione».

Cosa puoi dire in termini di presenza femminile alla prossima Biennale?

Angela Harutyunyan: «Sono rimasta profondamente colpita dallo straordinario team della Sharjah Art Foundation: la loro professionalità, la comprensione sensibile e sfaccettata dell’arte e degli artisti, e la capacità di gestire con calma e lucidità situazioni complesse. Sì, la maggior parte dei miei colleghi alla SAF sono donne, e trovo che siano incoraggiate a lavorare e agire in autonomia, a prendere l’iniziativa, e a farlo all’interno di un’istituzione che ha i suoi parametri e i suoi obiettivi, e che vanta una storia che risale a diversi decenni fa. Sono particolarmente colpita dalla loro sensibilità al contesto locale e dalla loro capacità di mediare tra i valori locali e quelli del pubblico globale, le forme estetiche e le aspettative».

Cosa hai portato dalla tua precedente esperienza curatoriale a questa Biennale?

Angela Harutyunyan: «Come ho accennato, provengo da un background accademico, e la Biennale è un luogo di ricerca e didattica, oltre che un’occasione per presentare l’arte contemporanea a un pubblico internazionale. Immagino di aver introdotto un metodo di lavoro piuttosto comune in ambito accademico: bisogna avere un’argomentazione coerente e suffragarla attingendo a diverse fonti. Questo non significa che il mio approccio alle opere d’arte sia puramente illustrativo. Tutt’altro.

Al contrario: pur avendo una concezione teorica e storica generale, seguo la “guida” dell’oggetto stesso, la sua storia di produzione e ricezione, la sua materialità, ciò che vuole fare nel mondo e il tipo di dialogo che intrattiene con le opere che lo hanno preceduto e con quelle contemporanee. Credo che la coerenza generale sia importante per me, così come mostrare i diversi modi in cui l’arte contemporanea viene mediata in contesti differenti. Come docente, mi interessa concepire la Biennale come un luogo di apprendimento e, insieme al Programma di Apprendimento, stiamo aprendo la Biennale a diverse comunità locali».

Che tipo di “eredità” vorresti lasciare a Sharjah dopo la sua Biennale?

Angela Harutyunyan : «Molto spesso, le tracce che un’opera lascia in vari luoghi e viene recepita in vari momenti vanno oltre le intenzioni degli autori. La ricezione dell’arte e della ricerca è complessa e si attiva in modo diverso a seconda delle circostanze storiche di chi le riceve. Una cosa, tuttavia, che spero di lasciare dopo la 17ª Biennale di Sharjah è la consapevolezza che essa rappresenti un “archivio” del nostro presente storicamente concepito, in modo che un ricercatore, uno studente o qualsiasi altra persona che viva a Sharjah e che in futuro si imbatta in queste tracce possa cogliere qualcosa del tempo in cui viviamo».

Paula Nascimento: «La Biennale di Sharjah è una delle biennali più importanti per gli artisti del Sud del mondo, ed è anche una piattaforma per promuovere il dialogo e altre forme di confronto. Da un lato, vorrei dare visibilità ad alcuni artisti che non sono stati spesso visti sulla scena internazionale e magari avere la possibilità di interagire con il loro lavoro. Dall’altro lato, pensando a spazi come la Global Studies University, l’Africa Institute, eccetera, è interessante capire come e quali dialoghi si possano instaurare con questo luogo e con l’Africa sud-occidentale, quali storie ci raggiungono».

Come descriveresti, in generale, l’atmosfera di Sharjah?

Angela Harutyunyan: «Ammiro molto gli sforzi intrapresi dalla Sharjah Art Foundation e da altre istituzioni statali e pubbliche per preservare e valorizzare il patrimonio culturale, sia materiale che immateriale, intendendo per cultura non solo l’alta cultura dei governanti, ma anche la cultura popolare delle diverse comunità che vivono nell’Emirato. Mi interessa inoltre osservare come si siano mossi con cautela nel turbolento panorama geopolitico e nei mutevoli equilibri della regione».

Paula Nascimento: «L’atmosfera di Sharjah è tranquilla, si percepisce un ritmo lento, cosa che apprezzo particolarmente. Provenendo da una città affacciata sul mare, l’onnipresenza dell’acqua e del mare rendono questo deserto un luogo speciale, un posto davvero affascinante, senza pretese e accogliente».

title_original: Alex Margo Arden Gets Up Close and Personal With Amy Winehouse’s Items for an Exhibition in London
editorial_title_zh: 亚历克斯·玛戈·阿登在伦敦举办展览，走近并细致呈现艾米·怀恩豪斯的私人物品
editorial_excerpt_zh: 今年夏天是艾米·怀恩豪斯逝世15周年。

Courtesy the artist and the Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "整个项目中对细节的敏感度令人惊叹。在这个长达5年的寻宝过程中，阿登曾一度拿到同一本书的20个版本；她想要比较每一本书的书脊和封面，以确保自己找到了正确的那一本。这一劳动的大部分成果在《Library》（2026）中得到了展示，其中包含弗拉基米尔·纳博科夫（Vladimir Nabokov）的《说吧，记忆》（Speak Memory）中的几十卷书，旁边是烹饪书《The New Classic 1000 Recipes》，离一本关于婚姻的书也不远。此外，还有关于大卫·贝克汉姆（David Beckham）、鲍勃·迪伦（Bob Dylan）、卡洛尔·金（Carole King）、玛丽莲·梦露（Marilyn Monroe）和奥黛丽·赫本（Audrey Hepburn）的传记。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我在艺术作品中想要表达的是，作为一个收藏系列，这为我们提供了对怀恩豪斯生平非常深刻的洞察，”阿登说道，同时警告不要过分聚焦于任何单一一本书。她指出了一本《Weight Watchers》（慧妍雅集/体重监察会）的书，有些人可能会将其与怀恩豪斯的饮食失调史联系起来，而她的饮食失调曾被英国小报放在显微镜下审视。“孤立来看，这些物件可能会被用来极力推行关于她的特定叙事，”她解释道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在下一个展厅里，阿登呈现了《Same Otherwise》（2026），这是对怀恩豪斯位于杰弗里斯广场2号（2 Jeffrey’s Place）家中壁炉的复原——正是在那里，她写出了获得格莱美奖的专辑《Back to Black》。就像怀恩豪斯生前那样，阿登在壁炉架上方摆放了有框的英国版《Vogue》杂志、来自《Betty and Veronica》的漫画书页，以及一张带有玛丽莲·梦露照片的镜子。但这位艺术家留下了空白，而这位音乐家原本在那些地方装裱了朋友和家人的私人照片。“这些空白传达了一种事物既存在又永远缺失的感觉，”她说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Alex-Margo-Arden-Perfume-said-to-have-belonged-to-Amy-Winehouse-I-IV-2024-2026.-Courtesy-the-artist-and-the-Nicoletta-Fiorucci-Foundation.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV] (2024-2026),", "caption": "Alex Margo Arden, Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV] , 2024–26.
