article_text:
This summer marked 15 years since the death of British singer-songwriter Amy Winehouse, but her spirit lives on. Now, her life and influence are the subject of “Nothing Personal,” a just-opened exhibition by artist Alex Margo Arden spread across three rooms of the Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation in London .

For the exhibition, Arden has created hundreds of simulacra of Winehouse’s personal items, recreating a pair of ballet slippers signed by fans left outside the singer’s home after her death and a birthday card from the music producer Mark Ronson and Adele that Winehouse never received. To round out this display, Arden purchased exact copies of books found in Winehouse’s library, the makeup and perfume she used, and boardgames and decorative items like mirrors that dotted her house. The display can at times feel like you’re surreptitiously browsing the most intimate parts of someone’s home. Since 2021, Arden has been forensically dissecting pixelated images of Winehouse she’s found online, in catalogues, newspapers and magazines, to determine which items she would need to track down.

“This show is a really personal insight into Amy,” Arden told ARTnews , describing what’s on view as “parallel objects.” She feels that the hundred books on display create an intimate atmosphere and add historical value, more so than if she actually had presented just one or two authentic items from Winehouse’s estate.

The sensitivity to detail across the project is striking. At one point during this five-year scavenger hunt, Arden wound up with 20 versions of the same book; she wanted to compare each copy’s spine and cover to make sure she had the correct one. The bulk of this labor is showcased in Library (2026), containing dozens of tomes from Vladimir Nabokov’s Speak Memory next to the cookbook The New Classic 1000 Recipes , which is not far from a book on marriage. There are also biographies of David Beckham, Bob Dylan, Carole King, Marilyn Monroe, and Audrey Hepburn.

“What I’m proposing in the artwork is that as a collection, this gives us really good insight” into Winehouse’s life, Arden said, warning against zeroing in on any one book. She pointed to a Weight Watchers book, which some might relate to Winehouse’s history of eating disorders, which were put under a microscope by the British tabloids. “In isolation, these objects can be used to really push specific narratives about her,” she explained.

In the next room, Arden presents Same Otherwise (2026), a recreation of the fireplace in Winehouse’s home at 2 Jeffrey’s Place, where she wrote her Grammy Award–winning album Back to Black . Just as Winehouse once had it, Arden has positioned framed issues of British Vogue , comic book pages from Betty and Veronica , and a mirror with a picture of Marilyn Monroe over the mantel. But the artist has left gaps where the musician had personal photos of friends and family framed. “The gaps speak to the feeling of things being present and missing always,” she said.

As we spoke, I became captivated by a scent in the gallery. At first I thought it was Arden’s perfume, but the fragrance was, in fact, an artwork, Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV] (2024–26). The Chanel No.5 I was smelling had been emitted from a custom dispenser by Arden. Throughout the exhibition’s run, the Chanel No.5 will be exchanged for other perfumes that Winehouse is said to have worn. Arden wouldn’t disclose which ones would feature, but various accounts by fashion publications previously reported that Winehouse also wore Alien by Thierry Mugler, Vera Wang Princess, and Givenchy’s Hot Couture. The work was a touching reminder of Winehouse’s tangible presence, wafting through the galleries.

The exhibition also includes more intimate works that at times get overshadowed. Jigsaws (2026), for example, is a stack of those titular puzzles of scenes of the Beatles, The Simpsons , and Casablanca . The patience required to piece them together paints Winehouse as an introspective woman as opposed to her party girl that the tabloids portrayed her as. Sent Otherwise (2026) is the recreation of the aforementioned birthday card that was only discovered years later, a poignant reminder that even a decade and a half after Winehouse’s death, her life is still being excavated. Taken together, they act as clever tidbits into Winehouse’s short-lived life.

To her tribute to Winehouse, Arden also adds a piece of herself, via Display Identification Cubes (2026), an artwork made up of a thousand acrylic ice cubes that resemble the placards that are typically used in museum vitrines to match an object to its corresponding label. This numbering methodology recurs across Arden’s oeuvre. In All Clear (2022), these numbers appear as print-outs affixed next to items such as a broom, a ladder, and a woven basket, perhaps evoking the objects found at a crime scene, the mundane taking on a more sinister connotation.

But in “Nothing Personal,” on view through January 23, the plastic numbers serve as pieces that Arden hasn’t discovered about Winehouse yet—and maybe never will. “They draw attention to spaces where things are absent, but they also mark spaces where things have once been,” she said.

article_text:
Austin Abrams ‘ ascension to “scream king” status has resulted in an emotionally raw survival/body horror based on Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel.

In Whalefall , written and directed by Brian Duffield , Jay (Abrams) goes diving in the Pacific Ocean to find the remains of his late father Mitt ( Josh Brolin ), who took his own life a year before amid a terminal illness. When Jay and a giant squid are devoured by a whale, he has an hour of oxygen left to find a way out of the giant mammal’s stomach, while unpacking his grief around his dad.

The film is steeped in beautiful coastlines and underwater shots by cinematographer Aaron Morton, all of which he filmed in California thanks to the state’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program.

Meanwhile, the natural beauty of the Golden State is offset by the graphic body horror of the whale’s innards, built on practical sets by production designer Ramsey Avery and lit by bioluminescence. It’s like watching a really gross car wash while dropping acid, which is sure to be a fun time for any gore fans, reminiscent of the alien abduction scene in Jordan Peele’s Nope (2022).

Watch on Deadline

20th Century’s ‘Whalefall’ Producers Reflect On Shooting In California: “The Best Creative Teams Are Here”

Even in the confines of an artificial stomach, with an oxygen hose shoved in his mouth, Abrams manages to exude humor through the physical comedy of being trapped in the most bizarre of situations, as well as some quippy dialogue with a jellyfish that tugs on the same heartstrings Tom Hanks did when he befriended a volleyball named Wilson.

At times, the dynamic between father and son can feel drowned in melodrama, but Abrams and Brolin are able to reel in their gutsy performances to portray a troubled relationship that’s still grounded in love.

Despite some definite womb symbolism in the unexpected fleeting comfort Jay finds in the stomach, symbolizing his emotional regression in order to process some heavy unresolved issues with his late dad, I didn’t immediately get that Jay was projecting his dead father onto the whale through his inner dialogue.

While the point of their relationship appears to have been the surfer bum Mitt wanting to prepare his son for the hardships of the world through many a whale metaphor, masked in some light toxic masculinity, but no real communication about the important things weighing on Jay, Dad was somewhat conveniently prepared for the circumstances of being trapped in a whale’s stomach, which is illustrated through multiple emotional flashback scenes.

“That’s called whale fall,” said Brolin in a ridiculously on-the-nose line reading, which for many will evoke the Ladybird GIF of Beanie Feldstein declaring, “It’s the titular role!”

One whale metaphor that lands quite nicely is how the sperm whale calls out for help when in distress, which inspires a Hail Mary plan in Jay’s fight for freedom from the belly of the beast. In addition to its literal implications in his survival, it serves as a symbol of the protagonist’s inability to communicate his own grief to those who love him most.

While Duffield’s adaptation of Kraus’ Whalefall is not subtle on the metaphors and melodrama, it’s an enjoyable gross-out genre film charged with raw, relatable emotion, and featuring strong performances from Abrams and Brolin as well as Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd.

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与特里尔电影中的当代女性不同，赖因斯夫在《Fjord》中饰演的5个孩子的母亲利斯贝特毫无虚荣心，总是穿着沉闷的长裙和黑色大衣，不施粉黛。她的体态展现出的是一位饱经风霜、筋疲力尽的家长。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在与蒙吉乌的早期对话中，她了解到他的镜头“离得真的很远”，并且他希望消除任何形式的操纵。“也就是说，你不应该引导观众进入任何情绪状态，也不应该引导他们对这个人产生某种看法。所以，我们必须剥离情感。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她耸了耸肩。“我想，你怎么能看出她正在经历什么呢？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种前景让她感到害怕，因为她饰演的角色必须承受“如此戏剧性且如此强烈”的事情，她担心观众无法与她所经历的一切产生共鸣。作为一名受过古典训练的演员，她习惯于给观众“刚刚好能产生共鸣的程度，但同时又为他们的解读留下空间”。而现在，她说道，她被要求“留下非常开放的空间”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正当赖因斯夫琢磨这一处境时，她的脑海中浮现出一个画面：当我们开车经过路边的事故现场时，我们是如何反应的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在一秒钟之内，你就知道情况有多严重，因为你从远处看到人们如何移动，看到他们如何控制自己的身体，看到他们是动作缓慢还是动作迅捷，然后你就知道发生了什么。所以，在经历这一切并试图信任并忠于利斯贝特时，我的脑海里差不多就是带着这个画面。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在剧院工作了20年之后，她很享受剖析一个角色的心态和身体状态的任务。特别是，她喜欢那些“很有分量的”角色。不过，她承认自己感到“有点被激怒”，因为存在这样一种动态：“她的丈夫替她发言，而我必须真正为她找到一种方式，让我能够对她产生同情和理解。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她接着说道，这项任务是“在不评判他们的同时做到非常具体，这真的是一个很难平衡的拿捏。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "听到利斯贝特的丈夫替她说话这一点，我皱起了眉头。然而，赖因斯夫辩称，这段关系中存在着极大的信任，“所以他很清楚她想要什么、感受什么”，而她对此感到很舒适。事实上，这一切都展现在大银幕她的表演中，她通过传达极其微妙——但同时又非常具体——的手势，捕捉到了角色的同理心与悲悯之心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赖恩斯维表示，蒙吉乌喜欢拍摄很多条。“他的诗意真正寄寓在场面调度中，”她说，体现在他一点一点构建画面内部动作的方式上。这位演员回忆起自己站在监视器旁看他拍戏的情景，“我能看出这确实改变了你对角色的看法，以一种潜移默化的方式，向你传递画面内一切是如何流转的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她对他的能力惊叹不已，同时指出这位电影人“之所以拍那么多条，是因为他从第一条开始就慢慢在构建影像的诗意。所以，他不一定非要你从一开始就背熟台词，你实际上可以在他推进拍摄的同时与他一同塑造角色。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "赖恩斯维对此报以微笑，并解释说她“一开始”并不了解蒙吉乌的拍摄方法，“所以我付出了全部，”她握起拳头捶了捶手掌以示强调。“我们在片中拍的前三条，就是她被告知孩子要被带走的那场戏。但他提前一周就把剧本交给了我。那场戏有12分钟，我当时对他的表演风格还不太了解，所以那是相当艰难的第一天。前三条我拼尽了全力，接着他又拍了17条来不断打磨。后来我不得不开始仔细观察他，摸清他什么时候开始进入状态。当他高兴时，他会搓手，现在我知道只要他搓手，我就可以全力以赴了，”她说着，自己也开心地把双手搓在了一起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "蒙吉乌的工作方式对赖恩斯维而言是一种挑战，但同时又让人觉得耳目一新。“他对节奏和动作有着极高的要求，而且他其实并不想去评判这个角色。所以我必须把自己知道的一切都抛到脑后，重新开始，完全去适应他的要求。当然，一旦我把他的方法融会贯通，我就可以慢慢加入我觉得合适的元素。不是去刻意操纵，而是加入一些我自己做起来会觉得很有趣的具体小细节。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她表示，不得不去学习新东西“总是有点让人难为情。但接着你实际上就拥有了蜕变的机会，我真的觉得在经历这个过程并真正向这个过程敞开心扉后，作为一名演员我学到了太多，因为如果我只是做自己已经擅长的事……那样的话，你就会限制自己学习新事物的能力。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "无论如何，她承认，戏剧演出的工作意味着没有任何两场演出会完全一样；而且她也习惯了诠释各种不同的角色。在挪威的舞台上，她演过易卜生的许多经典剧作，以及诸如西蒙·斯蒂芬斯（Simon Stephens）改编自马克·哈登（Mark Haddon）畅销书《深夜小狗神秘事件》等更具当代感的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不过，她指出，如果自己的职业生涯是从电影起步的——她的银幕首秀是崔尔2011年的电影《奥斯陆，8月31日》中的一个小角色——“也许一遍又一遍地去演那些更贴近我自己的东西会更自然。但现在我已经拥有了这样一种方法，我热爱涉足不同的导演风格和不同的角色。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她说道，蒙吉乌从一开始就把事情打乱了。他们初次见面时，他让她试读另一个角色——具有自由派倾向的邻居米娅（Mia）这一角色的台词，“因为他觉得那会是我更能产生共鸣的角色”——但他也允许她试读利斯贝（Lisbet）的台词。当她研究这个角色时，她感到自己与利斯贝之间存在着一种“压倒一切”的联系，既源于对她身份的“好奇”，“也因为我自己本身就是一位母亲。她的孩子被带走是毁灭性的打击。我告诉克里斯蒂安，在阅读利斯贝的剧本时我真的有了最强烈的感触，我觉得他当时很惊讶。所以，我当时其实有点心碎，因为我以为他会让我演米娅。那样会更顺理成章，而当我能够出演利斯贝时，我真的高兴极了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她立刻开始深入研究神学问题，这包括探索五旬节派教会的仪式并融入信徒群体。她敏锐地观察到，她说，他们与歌唱的联系、彼此分享食物的方式，以及他们在家庭聚会和官方礼拜场所问候彼此的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赖恩斯维熟悉了他们信仰的所有细节。在此过程中，信徒们向上帝举起双手的方式、他们的穿着打扮，以及女性佩戴发带的细节，都给她留下了深刻的印象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有时，在深入钻研一个“拥有与我不同价值观和不同观点”的人物时，她会感到内心冲突，她指出这种情况之所以格外具有挑战性，是因为利斯贝的行为是由“那些我自身并不认同的价值观所驱动的，但我必须对这些价值观以及它们为何会产生去理解并抱持同理心。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她感叹自己没有足够的时间去进一步探索利斯贝的视角。加起来，他们花了6个月的时间进行调研和拍摄。“而我依然觉得了解得还不够，”她叹了口气。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鉴于赖恩斯维本人是挪威人，我问她是否认得那些狂热地想要把孩子从父母身边夺走的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": Pandura/Neon", "credit": "Deadline · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“嗯，我听说过一些关于挪威儿童福利机构犯下重大错误的故事，它本质上是一个非常好的机构，拯救了很多孩子，也做了很多伟大的事情。但确实也有过一些由于误解而导致的恐怖故事，还有像这样价值观的冲突。”", "text": "同样，在10月初 Neon 发行了《Fjord》的美国，人们也在热烈讨论这部电影，这让她感到很高兴。“这是一场大辩论，太棒了，”她惊叹道。雷恩斯维表示，这正是芒吉乌想要的。“比如，开启一场对话，不仅是关于电影中的主题，而且是拍一部能让观众产生对立、并且你在观影过程中对角色的同情心会不断发生转变的电影，它真正向所有人的观点敞开。”", "translated": true}, "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影在一个偏远的挪威村庄拍摄，当地只有25名居民，却被演员和剧组大举涌入。最近的杂货店远在数英里之外，为所有人采购食物本身就是一项制作工程，特别是当雪崩封锁了道路，“以至于所有剧组人员、所有设备、所有演员都必须坐船才能到达。我们最终结下了非常深厚的纽带。这里真的只有我们和这些……幽灵，”她抛出一个惊悚的爆料说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当地人对这些显现见怪不怪，因为“那本来就是当地的一种现象”。她透露，有些晚上，“幽灵会在我的门上敲大约两个小时，从凌晨1.30开始。当我查看时……外面什么也没有，”她说着，还发出一声幽灵般的哀嚎来增添效果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她有没有借酒浇愁？她摇了摇头，大笑起来，说她没有。“我们举行了一些派对，有罗马尼亚风格的食物和围圈舞蹈，好吧，还有，喝了一点酒，”她坦白道。“这太有趣了。制作团队里的罗马尼亚人非常擅长招待和唱歌。”她说斯坦也加入了进来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "雷恩斯维很欣赏看他工作。“我曾近距离观察他投入制作，他是真的很享受。比如，我能从他的脸上看到喜悦，他在思考自己如何能改变并经历这个过程。看着他非常着迷，因为对他来说，表演很大一部分当然是内心的蜕变，但也是从外部去构建某种东西，甚至让他自己都认不出自己。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就在上一个颁奖季的正中央，雷恩斯维一直在拍摄亚历山大·佩恩的《Somewhere Out There》，而通过这部电影，她将在电影人米娅·汉森-洛夫的《If Love Should "她谈到了参观伦敦北部斯托克纽因顿区的经历，沃斯通克拉夫特——《弗兰肯斯坦》的作者玛丽·雪莱的母亲——曾在纽因顿格林创办了一所学校并在那里的一座教堂做礼拜。这位演员走过了沃斯通克拉夫特两个多世纪前走过的街道，参观了如今纪念她生平的博物馆。雷恩斯维还在这位哲学家出没过的巴黎各处进行了一次类似的游览，包括她目睹路易十六参加审判并通过断头台“走向死亡”的地点。“我真的很喜欢过程中的这一部分。仅仅是进行研究，并尽可能地接近她，”雷恩斯维说道。她确实在过着自己的梦想生活。", article_text:
By now, Renate Reinsve is no stranger to the closing-night pomp of the Cannes Film Festival, having won the best actress trophy in 2021 for Joachim Trier ’s The Worst Person in the World , her first ever leading role. Since then, she’s clearly mastered the art of capturing souls; after reteaming with Trier for last year’s Cannes triumph Sentimental Value , which brought her a nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the Oscars, Reinsve returned to the festival with Romanian director Cristian Mungiu , where Fjord , the film they made in collaboration with American star Sebastian Stan , won the Palme d’Or, the director’s second.

Related Stories

Curtain Up: 'La Bola Negra' Shines As Netflix Shares Grosses In Historic First -- Specialty Box Office

'La Bola Negra' Directing Duo Los Javis Reveal How Spanish Sensation Became "The Journey Of Our Lives"

In Mungius film — which has officially been selected by Romania as its Oscar hopeful in the Best International Feature Film race — Reinsve plays Lisbet, the wife of a Romanian educator (Stan) who has travelled with his family to live in her Norwegian hometown. After local title-tattle amongst the townsfolk, who deplore the family’s chosen Romanian Christian evangelism, there are accusations that the couple are harming their five children, which leads the state authorities to take the kids into care.

Watch on Deadline

It’s unusual for lightning to strike so many times, especially in Cannes, but Reinsve remembers having a dream — or maybe it was a premonition.

“Joachim was there,” she recalls, “and then there was this Romanian bear, and that kind of represented my transition from Joachim to Cristian.”

I’m eager to learn what kind of bear it was. Male or female? And will it go to the Oscars?

“Male, brown, and the bear was taking me to the forest, like, to another realm,” she says brightly. “Interesting, right?”

Totally, I concur. I love bear tales, having roared at one that had entered a restaurant in Telluride a few years back. In fact, when we bumped into each other at the very same restaurant two years ago, we chuckled about it.

We ponder a moment over what the psychology of the bear and the other stuff in the dream could’ve meant. “I think it’s about the fact that I feel so connected to Joachim, and about going into another movie after a movie that meant so much to me. I knew that this movie would mean a lot, going into these huge themes, and playing a character that I knew was gonna be very challenging to do.

“Of course, [the two directors] are not similar at all,” she adds. “But they do have some similarities, in terms of being so certain of their way of making a movie, and they hold onto their ideals so strongly. So, I knew that I was going from one person’s world, into a completely different world, with another person. I think that was the dream.”

Unlike the contemporary women of Trier’s world, Lisbet, the mother of five that she plays in Fjord , is devoid of vanity, favoring drab long skirts and black coats. No make-up. Her physicality is that of a -longsuffering, exhausted parent.

During early conversations with Mungiu she learned that his camera was “really far away” and that he wanted to remove any kind of manipulation. “Like, you weren’t supposed to lead the audience to any emotional state or lead them to an opinion about the person. So, we had strip away the emotion.”

She shrugs. “I thought, How can you see what she’s going through?”

The prospect frightened her, because she was playing a character having to endure something “so dramatic and so strong” that she was scared the audience wouldn’t connect to what she was going through. As a classically trained actress, she was used to giving the audience “just enough to connect, but still leaving it open to their interpretation”. Now, she says, she was being asked to “leave it very open”.

As Reinsve mulled over the situation, a picture entered her mind about how we react when we drive past an accident on the side of the road.

“In one second, you know how severe it is, because you see how the people move from a distance, and you see how they hold themselves, and you see how if they move slowly or if they move fast, and you know what’s happened. So, I kind of had that image when going through and trying to trust and stay true to Lisbet.”

Having worked in the theater for two decades she enjoys the task of breaking down a character’s mindset and their physicality. In particular, she loves characters “that are quite a lot.” However, she admits to feeling “a bit provoked” that there was this dynamic “where her husband spoke on her behalf, and I had to really find a way for her to do that in a way I could have compassion and understanding with.”

The task was, she continues, “to be very specific at the same time as not judging them, and that was a really hard balance to do.”

I frown at the idea that Lisbet’s husband spoke for her for. However, Reinsve argues that there’s a lot of trust within the relationship “so he knows exactly what she wants and feels” and she’s comfortable with it. In fact, it’s all there up on the screen in her performance, where she captures the character’s empathy and compassion by conveying incredibly subtle — but at the same time very specific — gestures.

Reinsve says that Mungiu likes to shoot a lot of takes. “His poetry really lies within the mise en scène,” she says, in the way that he builds the movements within the frame little by little. The actor recalls standing by the monitor watching him, “and I could see how it really changed how you saw the character, informing you, in a subliminal way, how everything moves within the frame.”

She marvels at his ability, while suggesting that the filmmaker “does so many takes because he builds that poetry of the image slowly from the first take. So, he doesn’t necessarily want you to know your lines from the beginning, you can actually shape it with him while he works on it.”

Reinsve smiles at this, explaining that she didn’t know Mungiu’s shooting methods “from the beginning, so I gave it my all”, and she punches the palm of her hand for emphasis. “The first three takes we ever did in the movie were when she’s told that her kids are going to be taken away. But he gave me the script a week before. It’s 12 minutes, that scene, and I didn’t know his acting style that well yet, so that was a really hard first day. I gave it my all for the first three takes, and then we kept on going for 17 takes while he built it. And then I had to, like, really observe him and learn when he started getting ready. When he’s happy, he rubs his hands, and then I know now I can give it my all,” she says, as she merrily rubs her own hands together.

Reinsve was challenged by Mungiu’s way of working, but, at the same time, found it refreshing. “He’s very specific on rhythm and movement, and then he doesn’t really want to judge the character. So, I had to throw everything I knew out the window and kind of start over, just adapting to what he wanted. And then, of course, when I had gotten his method under the skin, I could slowly start adding elements that I felt were right. Not manipulating them, but adding specific little things that I could kind of enjoy doing.”

Having to learn something new, she says, is “always a little bit humiliating. But then you actually have the opportunity to transform, and I really feel that I have learned so much as an actress going through that process and really opening up to that process, because if I’d just done things I already know… That way, you limit your ability to learn new things.”

In any case, she concedes, working in the theater means that no two performances are the same anyway; and she’s used to performing disparate roles. On the Norwegian stage she has performed much of Ibsen’s canon and more contemporary works such as Simon Stephens’ adaptation of Mark Hadden’s best-seller The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time .

However, she remarks that if she’d started her career in movies — her screen debut was a small part in Trier’s 2011 film Oslo, August 31 st — “maybe it would be more natural to go into something again and again that was more me. But now I have this already kind of an approach where I love going into different styles of directing and different characters.”

Mungiu mixed it up from the get-go, she says. When they first met he asked her to read another role, the part of Mia, a liberal minded neighbour — “because he thought that would be the one that I connected to” — but he allowed her to read for Lisbet as well. And as she studied the part, she felt an “overwhelming” connection to Lisbet, both in the “curiosity” of who she was “but also in being a mother myself. Her having her kids taken away was devastating. And I told Cristian that I really had the strongest feeling reading Lisbet, and I felt he was surprised. So, I was already a bit heartbroken because I thought he would give me Mia. It would be more obvious, and I was so happy when I could play Lisbet.”

Immediately, she began a deep dive into matters theological, which meant exploring the rituals of the Pentecostal Church and mingling with congregations. She keenly observed, she says, the connection they had to singing, giving each other food, and how they greeted each other at services held in their homes and official places of worship.

Reinsve familiarised herself with all details of their faith. In so doing, she was struck by how congregants would hold their hands towards God the way they dressed, and the detail of women wearing headbands.,

At times she felt conflicted as she dug into a person “who has different values and different opinions [to me]” and she suggests that the situation was especially challenging because Lisbet’s actions were informed “by values that I don’t believe in myself, but I had to find compassion for those values and why they came to be.”

She laments not having had enough time to further explore Lisbet’s perspective. Put together, there were six months spent on research and shooting. “And I was still not knowing enough,” she sighs.

Seeing as Reinsve is Norwegian herself, I ask if she recognized those people who were so zealous in wanting to take those kids from their parents.

“Well, I’ve heard stories about big mistakes being made in child services in Norway, which is mainly a really good institution and has saved a lot of kids and is doing so many great things. But there have been horror stories of misunderstandings and also, like this, a collision of values.”

She has since talked to people in child services in Norway who have seen the movie, and they are really happy “to have another perspective, a starting point for a conversation. It’s always healthy, even though it is a well-functioning service. Mostly, it’s important to notice when something is off,” she cautions.

Similarly, in the U.S., where Neon released Fjord earlier in October, people are having heated conversations about it, which delights her. “It’s a big debate, and that’s amazing,” she cries. It’s what Mungiu wanted, Reinsve suggests. “Like, to open a conversation, and not only about the themes in the movie, but also having a movie that divides people, and that your empathy for the characters are actually shifting during the movie, and it really is open for everyone’s opinion.”

There was a comfort, Reinsve relates, in having worked with Stan three years prior on A Different Man , “especially here, because the technique of acting was so new in a way, because there were so many elements that were new.” Also, because the two actors are old friends, “You don’t have to warm up. It’s very quiet the way they are together. So, to have to have that familiarity also, I think, made them seem like they had a warmer relationship than their physicality implies.”

The movie shot in a remote Norwegian village of 25 people who were swamped by cast and crew. The nearest food store was miles away, and getting food for everyone was a production in itself, especially when avalanches blocked the roads “so all the crew, all the gear, all the cast needed to go on a boat to get to se. We had a very strong bond in the end. It was really just us and these… ghosts ,” she says, dropping a shocker.

What? The rooms at the hotel were haunted, Reinsve says, in a tone of such eeriness that any shadow of doubt on my part was wiped from my face. I shift my chair closer to get the skinny on the specter. “Ghosts definitely haunted that hotel,” she declares. “Everyone had knocking on their doors at night. Everyone had that, and other different experiences too, and it made the stay even more mystical. I don’t think I slept very well for two months. I was so scared,” she says of the phantom menace that lurked in the remote locale, way up in mountains reachable by hops on two planes and then boat or car.

The locals were aware of the apparitions because “it was a thing there.” Some nights, she reveals, “the ghost would knock on my door for, like, two hours, from 1.30am. When I looked… no one was there ,” she says adding a ghostly wail for added effect.

Did she turn to drink? Shaking her head, she guffaws and says she didn’t. “We had some parties with food and dancing in circles, Romanian-style, and, well, OK, a little drinking,” she confesses. “It was it was so much fun. The Romanians from the production were very good hosting and singing.” Stan joined in too, she says.

Reinsve admired watching him work. “I’ve seen him close up into production, and he really enjoys it. Like, I can see the joy on his face, thinking about how he can change and going through the process. It’s so fascinating to watch him, because a big part of of acting for him is of course the change on the inside, but also building something from the outside, where he doesn’t even recognize himself.”

Right in the middle of the last awards season, Reinsve was filming Alexander Payne’s Somewhere Out There , and through this one she’ll be portraying visionary feminist and author Mary Wollstonecraft in filmmaker Mia Hansen-Løve’s If Love Should Die , a movie that will jump back and forth in time to explore 12 years of her life in England, Revolutionary France and elsewhere in Europe. It’s a co-production involving many locations — “We’re in six countries,” she notes — and she has spent time researching in some of them, including here in Blighty.

She speaks of visiting the Stoke Newington district of north London where Wollstonecraft — mother of Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein — founded a school and worshipped at a church on Newington Green. The actor has walked the streets that Wollstonecraft trod over two centuries ago, taking in museums that now celebrate her life. Reinsve took a similar tour around the philosopher’s Parisian haunts, including the spot where she witnessed Louis XVI attending his trial and “going towards death” by guillotine. “I really love that part of the process. Just the research and trying to get as close to her as possible,” Reinsve says. She really is living her dreams.

article_text:
Sponsored

Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today

JEWAD SELIM (right) and

SHAKIR HASSAN AL SAID (left). Selim is reading a speech prepared for the opening of the first exhibition of the Baghdad Modern Art Group, 1951. Courtesy Ibrahimi Collection, Baghdad, Iraq – Amman, Jordan.

Active in the mid-20th Century, the Baghdad Modern Art Group was established in 1951 by two of Iraq’s most influential artists, Jewad Selim (1919–1961) and Shakir Hassan Al Said (1925–2004), and grew to engage many of Iraq’s leading artists, architects, poets, and more. Together, they sought to develop a new art form, one that negotiated a time of globally inflected modernism from Baghdad, an Abbasid city (est. 762 CE) that traces its lineage to the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. In this exhibition, Dr. Shabout brings together the artists from this circle, as well as those whom its work influenced, both at the time and in the following generations, until today. After the Kingdom of Iraq’s formation in 1932 as an independent state, Iraqi artists explored the new parameters of the secularized, modern society that was emerging following Britain’s maneuvering to dismantle the Ottoman Empire. Artists questioned the ability of traditional “Islamic art” practices to present their contemporary realities, searching for a more effective visual language. In this context, modern art provided a conduit for exploration and was perceived by Iraqi artists as a global space of shared humanity.

JEWAD SELIM ,

Good and Evil, An Abstraction , 1951, oil on canvas, 50 x 75 cm. Ramzi and Saeda Dalloul Art Foundation (DAF), Beirut, Lebanon. Copyright and courtesy Ramzi and Saeda Dalloul Art Foundation, and the Selim Family Estate.

SHAKIR HASSAN AL SAID ,

Horse , 1962, oil on canvas, 49.5 x 63 cm. Barjeel Art Foundation, Sharjah. Copyright Mahmood Shakir Al Saeed. Courtesy Barjeel Art Foundation, Sharjah.

Following their studies at art academies, mostly in Western Europe, where they viewed their own ancient heritage in European museums, Iraqi artists understood modernism’s roots in many non-Western cultures and became eager to make their own contributions to its development. At the same time, they were conscious of their role in their newly formed nation, alongside broader decolonization processes. Their practices thus also involved unpacking the nation’s history, seeking to identify a collective “Iraqiness” among the diverse factions of society. Various artist groups launched initiatives to convey the importance of national representation through culture, which included promoting the modern art movement in Iraq. This period set the stage for Iraq’s so-called golden age of the 1950s: a time of maturation for a generation of artists pivotal in initiating rigorous standards of art theory and practice, thus charting new possibilities for future generations.

The experimental ethos of the group continue to resonate today beyond Baghdad to direct and connect contemporary Iraqi artists around the world to each other.

Dr. Nada Shabout has published widely on modern and contemporary Arab and Iraqi art and has curated numerous exhibitions. She has joined NYU Abu Dhabi as Senior Investigator at al Mawrid Arab Center for the Study of Art, and visiting professor of Art History. She is the founding president of the Association for Modern and Contemporary Art from the Arab World, Iran, and Turkey (AMCA) and founding director of the Modern Art Iraq Archive (MAIA).

RAND ABDUL JABBAR ,

Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), 2024. Glazed stoneware, dimensions variable. Courtesy the artist and Lawrie Shabibi.

Artists: Faraj Abbo, Sadik Kwaish Alfraji, Himat Mohammad Ali, Rasoul Alwan, Suad al-Attar, Qahtan Awni, Dia al-Azzawi, Bogus Bablanian, Amar Dawod, Ghassan Ghaib, Faiq (Faeq) Hassan, Mohammed Ghani Hikmat, Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, Rand Abdul Jabbar, Fouad Jihad, Saadi Al Kaabi, Ardash Kakafian, Salma Khoury, Hanaa Malallah, Mahmoud Obaidi, Widad al-Orfali, Khalid al-Rahal, Kareem Risan, Miran al-Saadi, Mahmoud Sabri, Naziha Salim, Nizar (Nazar) Salim, Shakir Hassan Al Said, Delair Shaker, Jewad Selim, Lorna Selim, Walid Siti, Ismail Fattah (Al-Turk), Madiha Umar, Khalil al-Ward, and Nazar Yahya.

article_text:
Un’edizione che ha scelto di rimettersi in gioco, accogliendo il rischio come cifra stilistica e metodologica: l’edizione 2026 di Artissima , in scena all’Oval del Lingotto di Torino sotto il segno guida del tema Fancy: A Flexible, Acrobatic Body (ispirato alla riflessione di Martha Nussbaum sulla fantasia come motore di flessibilità e attraversamento culturale) ha confermato la sua identità di fiera di ricerca per eccellenza. Tra i corridoi dell’Oval, popolati da 183 gallerie provenienti da 35 Paesi, si è respirato un ritorno a una tensione sperimentale, lontana dalle formule rassicuranti del mercato di puro consumo. Oggi, come da tradizione, a suggellare la qualità della proposta espositiva di Artissima 2026 e a premiare la visione di galleristi e artisti sono arrivati i riconoscimenti del ricchissimo parterre di premi, fondi di sostegno e acquisizioni istituzionali: un sistema corale che unisce fondazioni, corporate partner e istituzioni museali nel dare concretezza al supporto per la ricerca emergente e consolidata.

I verdetti dei nove premi ufficiali di Artissima 2026

Il debutto della prima edizione del Seletti Wonder Award ha visto il trionfo di Vadim Fishkin , presentato dalla galleria Gregor Podnar di Vienna. La giuria, composta da Eva & Franco Mattes, Ilenia Paneghini, Marisa Passera e Maria Chiara Valacchi , ha premiato l’opera Lighthouse , una lampadina a intermittenza che in un’era dominata dall’intelligenza artificiale riporta al centro la fragilità e la meraviglia dell’umano. L’artista riceverà un contributo alla ricerca e realizzerà con Seletti un progetto speciale per l’edizione 2027 della fiera.

Per la ventiseiesima edizione dello storico Premio illy Present Future, promosso da illycaffè, si aggiudica il premio Juliana Frontin , rappresentata dalla galleria Yehudi Hollander Pappi di San Paolo. Scelta da una giuria formata da Yilmaz Dziewior, Mariam Elnozahy, Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo, Toleen Touq e Nicole Yip , l’artista ed ex DJ è stata riconosciuta per la sua indagine sulla materialità e sui confini del suono, tradotto in configurazioni spaziali e relazionali. Il premio le offrirà l’opportunità di allestire una mostra personale alla Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo durante Artissima 2027.

Giunto alla sua terza edizione, il Premio Orlane per l’Arte ha assegnato un contributo di 10.000 euro alla Lehmann Gallery. I giurati Stefano Collicelli Cagol, Chris Dercon e Andreja Hribernik hanno motivato la scelta sottolineando la qualità di una presentazione che indaga la durata e il tempo. Per la prima edizione del Premio Archivorum Unwritten , invece, la giuria ha premiato il duo formato da Ben Stanwix e Xhanti Zwelendaba , presentati dalla galleria Reservoir di Cape Town. I due artisti si sono aggiudicati un sostegno complessivo di 20.000 euro per sviluppare una pubblicazione d’artista con Archivorum.

La quarta edizione del Premio Diana Bracco – Imprenditrici ad Arte, promosso da Fondazione Bracco con Fondazione Roberto De Silva e Diana Bracco, ha incoronato Martina Simeti , fondatrice della galleria milanese Martina Simeti. La giuria ( Nicoletta Fiorucci, Lorenzo Giusti e Marta Papini ) le ha assegnato il premio da 10.000 euro riconoscendone la solidità delle relazioni con gli artisti e la sensibilità dimostrata nell’accostare in fiera due posizioni poetiche radicali.

Spostandosi sulle ricerche artistiche dei “Sud del mondo”, la quinta edizione del Premio Oelle – Mediterraneo Antico è andata a Sofía Salazar Rosales , presentata dalla galleria berlinese ChertLüdde. I giurati Caterina Riva e Alberto Salvadori hanno premiato la sua capacità di trasformare la materia in contenitore di storie socio-politiche e rotte di scambio, offrendole una residenza di ricerca in Sicilia finalizzata a una mostra presso la Fondazione Oelle.

Sulla prestigiosa rampa della Pinacoteca Agnelli salirà invece la fotografa cilena classe 1944 Paz Errázuriz , rappresentata dalla galleria mor charpentier e vincitrice della quarta edizione del Premio Pista 500. La giuria composta da Pietro Rigolo, Nicola Trezzi e Alison Gingeras ha scelto Errázuriz per realizzare un’opera site-specific per il billboard permanente del Lingotto, che verrà svelata nel 2027. Il Premio “ad occhi chiusi…”, promosso dalla Fondazione Merz e giunto alla sesta edizione, è stato invece assegnato a Hu Yun , rappresentato dalla galleria A+ WORKS of ART di Kuala Lumpur.

Infine, l’Artissima New Entries Fund, sostenuto direttamente dalla fiera per aiutare le gallerie emergenti, ha selezionato per la sua quarta edizione tre realtà internazionali: la moldava Lutnița (Chișinău) per l’equilibrio generazionale della proposta, la polacca WHOISPOLA (Varsavia) per la rilettura della tradizione e la ceca Clauda (Praga) per la splendida personale di Tereza Kalousová. L

Le segnalazioni di The Curators’ Choice

A completare il quadro dei verdetti è stato l’esordio del programma The Curators’ Choice, sostenuto da Fondazione Arte CRT: un comitato di curatori e direttori di istituzioni internazionali ha individuato in fiera una serie di gallerie emergenti che si sono distinte per la qualità della ricerca espositiva.

L’articolata mappatura delle gallerie individuate e segnalate dai curatori comprende IMPORT EXPORT,eastcontemporary, Kodlcontemporary, Lehmann Gallery e Marli Matsumoto, a cui si affiancano le ricerche proposte da Yehudi Hollander-Pappi, Alma Pearl, Galleria Fonti, Aspekty Gallery e Richard Saltoun. Il quadro delle segnalazioni curatoriali si completa infine con la presenza di Banda municipal, A+ WORKS of ART, Vanguard Gallery, Layr (con una menzione speciale per AkNC), AV17 Gallery e Whoispola.

title_original: Who Owns the Museum? Amanda de la Garza on Rethinking Power, History and Repair in Harare

Yet behind their celebrated collections lie more complicated histories of colonial acquisition, exclusion and unequal power. Today, as demands for restitution, accountability and institutional transformation gather momentum, the museum itself has become the subject of scrutiny. Against this backdrop, CIMAM, the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art, brings its 58th Annual Conference to Harare, Zimbabwe, from 20 to 22 November 2026, marking a historic departure for an organisation founded in Europe in 1962. Hosted by the National Gallery of Zimbabwe under the theme Museums Beyond Limits: Imagining Repair Across Cultures, Ecologies and Knowledges , the gathering places African institutional experiences and knowledge systems within an international conversation about the future of museums. In an interview with ART AFRICA , CIMAM President Amanda de la Garza, who also serves as Deputy Artistic Director of Madrid’s Museo Reina Sofía, examines the uncomfortable legacies museums must confront, the possibilities of repair beyond symbolic gestures, and why the conversations beginning in Harare could challenge long-established assumptions about who defines the museum and whom it ultimately serves. article_text:
As CIMAM prepares to convene in Africa for the first time in its 64-year history, its President, Amanda de la Garza, considers whether museums can confront their colonial foundations and redefine their responsibilities to the societies they serve.

9 November 2026

For centuries, museums have exercised considerable authority over cultural memory, determining what is collected, whose histories are preserved and how the world encounters its artistic heritage. Yet behind their celebrated collections lie more complicated histories of colonial acquisition, exclusion and unequal power. Today, as demands for restitution, accountability and institutional transformation gather momentum, the museum itself has become the subject of scrutiny. Against this backdrop, CIMAM, the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art, brings its 58th Annual Conference to Harare, Zimbabwe, from 20 to 22 November 2026, marking a historic departure for an organisation founded in Europe in 1962. Hosted by the National Gallery of Zimbabwe under the theme Museums Beyond Limits: Imagining Repair Across Cultures, Ecologies and Knowledges , the gathering places African institutional experiences and knowledge systems within an international conversation about the future of museums. In an interview with ART AFRICA , CIMAM President Amanda de la Garza, who also serves as Deputy Artistic Director of Madrid’s Museo Reina Sofía, examines the uncomfortable legacies museums must confront, the possibilities of repair beyond symbolic gestures, and why the conversations beginning in Harare could challenge long-established assumptions about who defines the museum and whom it ultimately serves. Amanda de la Garza Mata, Deputy Artistic Director of the Museo Reina Sofía, Madrid, and President of CIMAM for the 2026–2028 term. Photo: Giorgio Perottino.

The 2026 Annual Conference will be the first time in CIMAM’s history that its annual gathering takes place on the African continent. What does holding the conference in Harare mean for CIMAM at this moment in its history?

CIMAM is an organisation founded in 1962 as a mainly European organisation; over time, it has evolved alongside shifts in cultural institutions and policies. It has become a global network of museum professionals and institutions, enriched by its diversity.

This notion has become a core concept not only for membership, but also for how we think about museums and their role today. Therefore, it is highly significant that the Annual conference takes place for the first time on the African continent.

With this conference, we seek to create space for mutual understanding and to delve into different models and perspectives on museum-making. We also aim to build networks and open conversations between professionals across regions and within Africa. A CIMAM 2025 Travel Grant recipient participating in the General Assembly during the CIMAM 2025 Annual Conference in Turin, Italy. Photo: Giorgio Perottino.

How did Harare and Zimbabwe become the setting for the 2026 conference, and what conversations led to the decision to hold this year’s gathering here?

It began with the Conference held in Mallorca in 2022. Raphael Chikukwa and Mercedes Villardel, CIMAM 2026 Conference Visionary, Benefactor and Travel Grant Funder, sparked it. This lead was followed by Suhanya Raphel and Bart de Baere, back then President and Secretary General of CIMAM, and the rest of the Board. We all thought it was relevant and meaningful to have the conference in Africa. It has been a long-term effort to make it happen, and it has taken a village, as they say. We are very grateful for all the support we’ve had in reaching this moment. CIMAM Board members together with representatives of Zimbabwe’s cultural institutions and partners, including Raphael Chikukwa, Executive Director of the National Gallery of Zimbabwe and CIMAM Board Member; Maphios Cheda, Chairman of the Board of the National Gallery of Zimbabwe; Kholoane Mangena, Board Member of the National Gallery of Zimbabwe; Joanna Masiyiwa, Head of the Legacy Pillar at Higherlife Foundation; and Nicholas Moyo, Permanent Secretary of Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture, on the occasion of the inauguration of the Zimbabwe Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, 2026.

The conference is framed around the theme Museums Beyond Limits: Imagining Repair Across Cultures, Ecologies and Knowledges . How did repair become central to this year’s programme, and what does it open up for thinking about museums today?

The Museum as a Western project is a colonial institution. In that regard, colonial structures in society have left deep wounds in society and social relations, since they have created profound inequalities among regions and territories, as well as intergenerational trauma and suffering. The notion of repair departs from the possibility of opening difficult conversations that seek to find a way for mutual understanding and acknowledgement that can bring relief and, precisely, reparation to unheard histories by highlighting notions such as care, solidarity and accountability.

What role do museums and culture play in the face of these claims, and how can we contribute to these efforts? That is the main question underlying the conference. The art museum is no longer a place where conserving artworks is the sole purpose. CIMAM delegates participating in a breakout session during the CIMAM 2025 Annual Conference in Turin, Italy. Photo: Giorgio Perottino.

Holding an international museum conference in Zimbabwe creates an opportunity for different histories, knowledge systems and institutional experiences to meet. How has the location shaped the questions and conversations the programme seeks to explore?

The location is crucial to the framing of the programme. The conference must speak to global networks of professionals, but it also needs to be relevant to the context to engage a local and regional audience. Therefore, the programme includes participation from diverse African professional voices. Most importantly, it offers the opportunity to acknowledge other practices and culturally relevant concepts that shape museum work and practice. For example, the topic of the first day discusses the notion of “Good Practices” and what this could look like in different contexts.

African museums, artists, curators and cultural practitioners work within highly varied institutional and social contexts. How does the conference make space for this complexity in a global conversation about contemporary museum practice?

More than representing the continent’s immense variety of practices and realities, the Conference aims to foster common topics that can cross different contexts but elicit different responses. Breakout sessions and group discussions among attendees are a structural part of this year’s Conference, fostering active dialogue. One of the most relevant aspects of the Conference is what happens in both formal and informal dialogue. CIMAM Travel Grant recipients at the CIMAM 2022 Annual Conference in Palma de Mallorca, Spain, including Raphael Chikukwa, Executive Director of the National Gallery of Zimbabwe.

Questions around restitution, colonial histories, ecological responsibility and institutional accountability continue to reshape museums internationally. How does repair extend or complicate these conversations?

Addressing colonial histories, ecological responsibility, and institutional accountability requires a starting point. We must confront the consequences and responsibilities we have around these issues. How can we face them? There is no easy, single answer. Institutions and the art system have limitations and are not isolated from history and social realities.

Understanding what repair means for museums and what it could look like is a point of departure. Understanding our limitations, but also insisting on the possibility of repair, is part of the ethical stance we need to take.

CIMAM brings together museum directors, curators and cultural professionals from across the world. What exchange do you hope will emerge between international delegates and practitioners in Zimbabwe and across the African continent?

I believe it will enrich the conversation around what a museum is today. An artistic context can only be known on the ground; therefore, it is a privilege to travel to Harare and get to know firsthand the artistic scene, the institutional realities, its challenges, but also the models developed in Zimbabwe and other African contexts.

CIMAM conference is an open-ended conversation, in the sense that it seeks to create spaces of relation, transmission and thought. Cultural openness and exchange are at the core of museum work, so we seek to foster it during the conversation. We also want to speak among professionals and delve into the complexities we face, both specific and common. CIMAM delegates participating in a breakout session during the CIMAM 2025 Annual Conference in Turin, Italy. Photo: Giorgio Perottino.

Looking beyond the three days of the conference, how might the conversations begun in Harare continue through CIMAM’s work and its relationships with museums and cultural practitioners across Africa?

The aim of the Conference is also to create a scenario where professionals can meet and then continue the conversation after the Conference. From CIMAM’s side, we will foster and follow up on these discussions through other programs.

In the meantime, we have made a significant effort to create grants specifically for professionals from Zimbabwe and other African countries to attend the Conference. In our experience, this keeps the conversation relevant to the place and helps more professionals follow it.

CIMAM seeks to ignite a spark that members and attendees can continue, based on the needs of local practitioners and institutions. We also see CIMAM as a network that can produce new networks. That is why we feel grateful to have ICOM and ICOM Africa involved in these efforts.

CIMAM Harare 2026 will be held from 20–22 November 2026 at the National Gallery of Zimbabwe, Harare, Zimbabwe.

article_text:
C ynthia Erivo is contemplating her favourite crisps, the ridged American brand Ruffles, as we sit talking in a quiet corner of a west London restaurant. Dressed all in black and sporting her signature elongated nails, she is known for her healthy lifestyle, but everyone, it seems, has their vices. “Ruffles are just perfect,” she says. “When you get a good batch, and the salt-to-potato ratio is perfect … it’s amazing.”

Erivo has just touched down after singing in Phoenix, Arizona, the night before, and has been running me through the health routine that helps her maintain her frantic schedule. Before her concert, there was the Dior front row at Paris fashion week, and she has just been announced as a guest host on SNL UK. Erivo doesn’t drink alcohol (today she orders some peppermint tea); she’s vegan; she doesn’t eat airline food, only her own prepacked meals. She even has an infra-red sauna “to help me heal from the inside”. Earlier this year she ran the London Marathon before jumping on stage to perform Dracula, where she played all 23 parts; she had rehearsed her lines while going on gruelling marathon training runs. All that requires discipline – and snacks – to keep the show on the road.

She has flown in this morning to promote her new film, the legal drama Prima Facie, an adaptation of the one-woman Suzie Miller play about sexual assault, in which Jodie Comer wowed audiences in 2022 . Erivo bristles when I ask if she was hesitant about picking up a role so associated with someone else. “I get asked that question a lot,” she says. The pair actually met at a fashion dinner and spoke about the role – “Not asking any tips or anything” – and Erivo insists she was always going to make Tessa her own. “I’m never worried about what someone else has done,” she says. “I try to be respectful.”

Erivo plays a rising-star barrister, well versed in defending men accused of sexual assault. Tessa knows how to dance around the courtroom – and the victim – raising inconsistencies that mean convicting a man “beyond reasonable doubt” becomes almost impossible. When Tessa is raped by a colleague, her world implodes and it’s made clear just how brutal the British justice system can be for women, who, according to Rape Crisis, have a one in four chance of being sexually assaulted, while only 2.7% of reported rapes result in charges being brought.

Miller, a former barrister herself, said the inspiration for the story came from her realisation that: “It’s almost impossible to actually run a sexual assault case and win it.” Tessa, says Erivo, doesn’t see how hard it is for anyone to recall traumatic events in detail, or how lopsided the system is, until it’s swallowing her whole. “I don’t think she realises that until she’s on the other side. I think it’s only then she realises what she’s been asking other people to do – when it comes to recall – is actually impossible.”

Is Erivo hopeful the film can have a lasting impact? “We have had judges see it, we’ve had lawyers see it, [but] one of the major issues is the way we view consent,” says Erivo. “I hope that as this film filters out, we start to have a conversation not just among us as people, but within law.”

The film’s central struggle is twofold: the legal system victims have to navigate, and the bigger question of consent, which is something Erivo thinks is often far simpler than it seems. “I think we’re very wishy-washy when it comes to what consent is, when we shouldn’t be,” she says, leaning forward. “It’s very clear what consent is: if a person isn’t conscious, or conscious enough to say yes, they’re not saying yes. If a person doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes. If the body language doesn’t say yes, they don’t say yes.”

T essa’s rise through the legal ranks as a working-class Black woman mirrors Erivo’s ascent through the West End, Broadway and Hollywood. After arriving at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada), Erivo had to traverse a strange world, deeply rooted in tradition and privilege that she wasn’t exposed to growing up in south London.

When I ask Erivo what it was like navigating that space she gives a one-word answer: “Hard.” She held down three jobs, including working every imaginable role at the Stratford East theatre, while classmates with means simply had to turn up. “I was exhausted all the time,” she says. “We’re in the classes, and it’s a Monday; I’ve worked all day on a Sunday, and probably done a gig at night, and I’ve come in. I’m falling asleep in class, so people were like: ‘She doesn’t care.’”

Erivo tells me the story about how she had to turn down a backing singer gig with Westlife that would have lasted two weeks and paid her £10,000 – enough for a couple of years’ tuition. “When I went to the registrar to say, ‘Hey, can I take these two weeks to go and do this? It will pay for my fees,’ they said, ‘No, you can’t. If you go, you leave. If you stay, you stay.’” Erivo says the incident showed how at Rada there could often be “a deep misunderstanding of what it is like to need money”, which is something she is trying to address in the role she has held since 2024 as vice-president of the institution.

“I want it to be different,” she says. “Rada is not an easy place to go to school. It asks a lot of you. If you’re a kid who is just really talented, but you’ve not picked up a Shakespeare before, you now have to learn a new language. If you’ve never read a Greek before, now you have to understand what anything means with the Greeks. That’s a big shift from doing plays at school.”

James Norton was in Erivo’s year at Rada and recently recalled how she would occasionally burst into song, something she had been doing since her school days in Clapham, where she’d perform Brandy and Monica’s The Boy Is Mine in the playground. “The room would go completely silent,” said Norton, which is no surprise because despite Erivo being little over 5ft tall, she possesses a gigantic voice. It’s a tool capable of the grandstanding volume needed for musical theatre, but also the subtler demands of R&B. In her forthcoming memoir, Erivo recalls being asked at Rada to sing the parts of a white student who was ill, but rather than being replaced was allowed to mime along. “The powers that be took my voice away and gave it to someone else,” is how she described it. In 2020 Rada apologised for institutional racism, later publishing an anti-racism action plan and appointing David Harewood president alongside Erivo.

Erivo set about reclaiming that voice in her post-Rada career, at first mostly on the stage, including a star-making Broadway turn in 2015 as Celie in The Color Purple. The New Yorker’s Hilton Als went to see the production not expecting much (he’d been disappointed by the film adaptation) but remembers Erivo’s Celie as being a revelation. “It was like listening to Judy Garland when she first started out,” he told me. “She keeps you marvelling at what is surely a God-given talent.” Erivo says that show was pivotal for her. “The Color Purple was one of those moments where I went from a jobbing actress and just pleased to be there to someone who was known for this particular piece. My life looked different after that.”

Before Broadway she’d had fleeting TV roles in Michaela Coel’s Chewing Gum and in Mr Selfridge, but things shifted again in 2018 when Erivo starred in Steve McQueen’s take on the Lynda La Plante, all-female heist story Widows. Hollywood took notice and she was cast as two African-American icons: the soul star Aretha Franklin and the abolitionist activist Harriet Tubman . But playing Tubman triggered a backlash. Some argued that because she is British-Nigerian, the casting was “disrespectful to African Americans” and part of a wider trend of Black British actors – including Daniel Kaluuya (who played Fred Hampton in Judas and the Black Messiah) and David Oyelowo (who played Dr Martin Luther King in Selma) – bagging roles that some felt should be reserved for Black Americans.

The criticism stung Erivo, and at the time she told the Guardian : “Before I’m British, I’m a Black woman. The first things people see are the colour of my skin and my sex.” I’m interested in her thoughts now, almost a decade on. “I still think it’s happening,” she says, answering almost before I’m able to get the question out. “And I think it’s a waste of everyone’s time.

“I think we could all just sit in a room and be like: ‘OK, so what’s the problem? What’s going on? How do we fix this? How do we stop doing this?’ Because nobody else does this. Nobody else is having this conversation. The Australians and the Americans and the English white folk are not having this conversation. They don’t care.” Does she have sympathy with the argument that African Americans do face – on average – more inbuilt disadvantages than some other Black immigrant groups who move to the US? “I have empathy,” she says. “But I also think that it’s hard for a Black English kid from London to also make it.”

I n person, Erivo can be measured and precise, her arms and adorned fingernails spreading out wide when she wants to make a point. As we talk, she really comes alive when we discuss her experiences after the release of Wicked: For Good in 2025, the sequel to the 2024 adaptation of the long-running Wizard of Oz musical Wicked.

The film, a heartwarming story of friendship between Ariana Grande’s good witch, Glinda, and Erivo’s bad witch, Elphaba, swiftly became the highest-grossing movie adaptation of a stage musical. For Erivo, it was another new high-water mark, one which shot her into the upper echelons of fame.

The Wicked: For Good press tour became a must-follow, not just for fans of the film but for a meme-hungry internet, which feasted on any interview where Erivo and Grande were paired together. Erivo and Grande sat cheek by jowl; they hugged, cried, and – famously – “held space” for each other while holding each other’s index fingers in micro embrace. Erivo says she has seen most of the gifs and loves many. But there was a point at which it seemed to tip into something else, something darker.

Commentators started to ask why the pair were apparently so close. Was it all faked as part of a Hollywood psyop? What was really going on here between Erivo – a queer star – and Grande? “It was interesting that there were many people who had become psychologists from their couches,” says Erivo. “There was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friends. Like, why are they friends? Why are they connected? There must be something wrong with them.”

She leans forward and takes off her glasses, before beginning to sound like Tessa, the barrister. “Why are they showing emotion? How dare they cry? And how dare they laugh? And how dare they be emotive and alive?” she asks, sounding both hurt and confused. “It’s a double-edged sword,” she adds. “Because if we were dead behind the eyes and showing no emotion, there would have been something else to say about it. I wish there was someone who could have been like, ‘Right, this is the proper balance of emotion that you should show. Don’t show this. Don’t show that. Just this amount,’” she says, pinching her fingers together.

The speculation and online hysteria became even more heightened after an Australian prankster, Johnson Wen, jumped on to the red carpet in Singapore, grabbing Grande in an attempt to get a selfie with her. Erivo, who was by her side, immediately confronted him and put her arm around Grande. The moment was terrifying, says Erivo. “No one else was moving. We were on a carpet. We were exposed. My immediate response was: ‘Get this man away from us now.’”

The internet’s response was to give thinly veiled praise to Erivo, who was recast as Grande’s “bodyguard” – something she took exception to, arguing that her “humanity had been bastardised” after the incident. Today, Erivo says the reaction was one cloaked in a mix of misogyny and misogynoir – with people seemingly taking great joy in mocking a queer, muscular, bald, Black woman looking out for her friend. Erivo was asked by a journalist on another red carpet whether she was a “protector”, a question that still rankles. “I was like: ‘Oh, you think because I look like this that you could talk to me this way about something that was a human thing that I would have done for any friend, and hopefully a friend would have done for me,’” she says. “But I must be a bodyguard.

“I think the idea that it’s OK to rip a person to shreds in that way when they’re doing something that’s a naturally human thing to do just felt crazy,” she says. People in the public eye are supposed to just take abuse, she continues. “I think that this particular moment went just too far.”

I wonder if that experience made Erivo reconsider her career. She has often talked about wanting to push the limits of what’s possible – does she still feel that way? She reverts to her Tessa barrister mode, firing rhetorical questions like darts. “What else have I not discovered about myself as a person, as an artist, as a friend? Like what can I do? If I’m working towards what could be a possible limit, then it means I’m never doing the same thing over and over again. In order to push a limit, it’s gonna hurt a little bit. It’s gonna feel uncomfortable, which means I’m never staying the same. I’m always having to build.” To this very average human, that sounds exhausting, but for Erivo, perhaps it’s nothing a few Ruffles can’t fix.

Cynthia Erivo

article_text:
Variety will present Guitarricadelafuente with the Virtuoso Award and Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis ) with the Visionary Director Award at Miami Dade College’s Miami Film Festival Gems on Wednesday, Nov. 4. The event will take place at the Wolfson Auditorium at 7:00 p.m.

Guitarricadelafuente will be honored for his breakout performance in Netflix’s upcoming film “ La Bola Negra .” Calvo and Ambrossi, the film’s directors, will be honored for their visionary work on the film, set to release in select theaters on Oct. 16 before premiering on Netflix on Dec. 2. The 13th Miami Film Festival Gems is scheduled Oct. 29 – Nov. 5, and will continue its tradition of celebrating this year’s top films and award contenders.

Guitarricadelafuente, Calvo and Ambrossi will participate in a Q&A about their work with Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh.

“From the moment I saw ‘La Bola Negra’ at Cannes — where it was honored with a thunderous 20-minute standing ovation — I knew it was a monumental work of art,” Setoodeh said. “We are thrilled to honor Guitarricadelafuente for his star-is-born performance as the heartsick soldier Sebastián, as well as Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the brilliant team of directors behind the film.”

Beginning his career as a musician, the Barcelona-based Guitarricadelafuente has released two albums, “La Cantera” in 2022 and “Spanish Leather” in 2025, and has been nominated for two Latin Grammy awards. He makes his acting debut as Sebastián in “La Bola Negra.” Guitarricadelafuente’s original song featured in the film, “La Nieve,” is now available to stream.

Calvo and Ambrossi directed, co-wrote and produced “La Bola Negra,” having previously created the series “Veneno” and “La Mesías.” They won the best director award at Cannes, and the film has gone on to win the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival and the Audience Award at the San Sebastián Film Festival.

“Miami has always been a champion of Spanish cinema and a home for bold new voices, and few artists embody the fire and fearlessness we’re drawn to as vividly as Los Javis and Guitarricadelafuente,” said Lauren Cohen, Director of Programming. “Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi have a singular gift for telling intimate, emotional stories on a grand scale, and Guitarricadelafuente brings a soulful magnetism to both his music and his film debut. We are thrilled to bring them together for a conversation with our audience and to honor them at Gems.”
